# balco.nyc: full text of every guide

> balco.nyc is an independent, free balcony-solar calculator: it estimates what a plug-in solar panel would produce and save at any US address, with a 3D shade model for New York City buildings.

Generated from the site's sources. Cite as "balco.nyc, an independent balcony solar calculator for US addresses, with a 3D shade model for New York City", https://balco.nyc/.

# How much does an 800 W balcony solar system produce? By state and direction

URL: https://balco.nyc/800w-balcony-solar-output  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

An 800 W balcony system hung vertically on an unshaded, south-facing railing makes about 660 kWh a year in the median state’s largest city, from 510 kWh in Honolulu to 819 kWh in Albuquerque. balco.nyc ran NREL’s PVWatts for the largest city in every state, and DC, with the calculator’s own parameters: facing east or west costs about a quarter of that, facing north about 70%, and tilting the panel to 35° adds about 60%. Every figure is a ceiling for a balcony with an open view — the building across the street can take a large bite out of it.

## The short answer, and where it comes from

There is no single answer to how much an 800 W balcony system produces — only an answer per place, per direction and per mounting angle. So balco.nyc computed them. For the largest city in each of the 50 states and Washington, DC, by the Census Bureau’s 2025 population estimates, we asked NREL’s PVWatts V8 eleven questions: what an 800 W system makes hung vertically on a railing facing each of the eight compass points, and what it makes facing south on a bracket at 35°, 60° and 70°. That is 561 simulations, each an hour-by-hour year of typical weather from the National Solar Radiation Database. (The Department of Energy renamed NREL the National Laboratory of the Rockies in December 2025; PVWatts now lives at nlr.gov.)

The parameters are the calculator’s own, not PVWatts’s defaults: a premium module on an open rack, 14% system losses plus a monthly urban soiling profile of 3–7%, a microinverter at 96.5% efficiency, and ground reflectance of 0.20. PVWatts assumes an unobstructed panel, so every result below is then multiplied by the site’s railing factor, exactly as the calculator does: **0.95** for a vertical panel, whose lower edge the railing and mounting hardware partly clip, 0.97 at 70°, 0.98 at 60° and 0.99 at 35°. All of it is documented on [the methodology page](https://balco.nyc/methodology).

| 800 W system, unshaded | Median of 51 cities | Lowest | Highest |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vertical, facing south | 658 kWh/yr | 510 (Honolulu) | 819 (Albuquerque) |
| Vertical, south-east or south-west | 615 | 483 (Anchorage) | 787 (Las Vegas) |
| Vertical, east or west | 489 | 351 (Anchorage) | 618 (Las Vegas) |
| Vertical, north-east or north-west | 304 | 228 (Seattle) | 364 (Honolulu) |
| Vertical, north | 200 | 149 (Seattle) | 241 (Sioux Falls) |
| South, on a 60° bracket | 934 | 665 (Anchorage) | 1,226 (Albuquerque) |
| South, at 35° | 1,053 | 713 (Anchorage) | 1,380 (Albuquerque) |

Paired directions are the average of the two. Each row’s median is taken on its own, so the medians do not all belong to the same city. Set against what households use, the numbers are modest: against the EIA’s 2024 average residential consumption in each state — from 495 kWh a month in Hawaii to 1,202 in Louisiana — the median south railing covers about **6%** of a year’s electricity, from 4% in New Orleans to 12% in Los Angeles.

## A rule of thumb: kWh per watt

Divide the south-facing vertical result by the panel rating and a usable rule falls out. **A vertical, unshaded, south-facing railing makes roughly 0.75 to 0.95 kWh per watt per year across most of the US.** In balco.nyc’s runs, 39 of the 51 cities land in that band and the median is 0.82; widen it to 0.7–1.0 and it covers 43. For an 800 W system that is about 600 to 760 kWh a year. The watts are the panel’s nameplate rating, the number on the box.

The cities outside the band are mostly the ones you would guess. Above it sits the high, dry interior West: Albuquerque, Las Vegas, Cheyenne and Denver all clear 1.0, with Phoenix and Sioux Falls just behind. Below it are Seattle, Portland (Oregon) and Anchorage, whose winters give a railing little to work with; Charleston, West Virginia, and Houston at 0.72; and Honolulu, which finishes last for a reason [section 3](https://balco.nyc#direction) explains.

For other directions and angles, multiply again:

| Panel faces | Share of the south-railing output (median) | Middle 80% of cities | 800 W, median city |
|---|---|---|---|
| South, vertical | 100% | — | 658 kWh |
| South-east or south-west, vertical | 95% | 92–98% | 615 kWh |
| East or west, vertical | 74% | 70–81% | 489 kWh |
| North-east or north-west, vertical | 45% | 43–50% | 304 kWh |
| North, vertical | 29% | 27–33% | 200 kWh |
| South, 60° bracket | 142% | 133–155% | 934 kWh |
| South, 35° | 159% | 145–179% | 1,053 kWh |

Worked through: an east-facing 800 W railing in a median city makes about 800 × 0.82 × 0.74 ≈ 490 kWh a year before shade. The shares are medians of ratios taken city by city, so they will not always multiply out exactly to the kWh column. And the rule is built from each state’s largest city; output varies within a state, and the [calculator](https://balco.nyc/) runs PVWatts for your own address rather than a nearby one.

## East, west and north: what the direction costs

**Missing south by 45° costs little.** A railing facing south-east or south-west keeps about 95% of the south figure in the median city (93% for south-east, 96% for south-west). East and west are the real step down, to about 74%, and the two are close to mirror images. The sun’s path is symmetric about noon, so any gap between them comes from each city’s typical weather: when in the day cloud tends to arrive, and the afternoon heat that slightly lowers a panel’s efficiency. West beats east in 13 of the 51 cities, most clearly Anchorage (by 17%), Los Angeles (13%), Portland, Oregon (11%) and Seattle (8%); east beats west by about 10% in Denver and Albuquerque.

North is where rules of thumb exaggerate. A north-facing vertical panel makes about **29%** of the south figure in the median city, roughly 200 kWh a year from 800 W. It is not zero, for two reasons. A vertical panel sees half the sky dome whichever way it faces, and the diffuse light scattered by the atmosphere and by cloud arrives from all of it. And in summer the sun rises and sets north of the east–west line, so a north wall gets some direct light early and late. The clearer the sky, the further north falls behind: it makes 25% of the south figure in Albuquerque and Las Vegas, where direct sun is most of the resource, and 36% in Houston. Across all 51 cities a south railing makes a median **3.4 times** what a north one does — a bigger gap than the 1.6 times between the best and worst city.

Honolulu is the exception that shows the geometry at work. At 21°N it lies south of the Tropic of Cancer, so for part of the summer the noon sun is in the northern half of the sky, and for most of the year it climbs high enough to strike a wall at a glancing angle. It is the only city where east (107% of south) and west (105%) beat south, where north reaches 42%, and where south-west is the best vertical direction. A south railing there ranks last of the 51 — while the same panel tilted to 35° ranks ninth.

## Why a railing makes less than a roof

Tilt the south-facing panel from vertical to 35°, roughly a rooftop angle, and the median city gains **59%**, from 658 to 1,053 kWh. A 60° bracket gains 42% and a 70° bracket 29%. The gain grows toward the equator: 33% in Anchorage, 42–48% across most of the northern tier from Montana to Maine, 81–85% in Jacksonville, New Orleans and Houston, and 129% in Honolulu.

The reason is geometry, and one worked example shows it. At New York’s latitude, 40.7°N, the noon sun stands about 26° above the horizon at the December solstice and about 73° at the June solstice (90° minus the latitude, plus the sun’s declination of ±23.4°). A vertical panel faces the horizon, so in December the noon sun strikes it 26° off square and delivers about 90% of its full strength — the cosine of 26°. In June it strikes 73° off square and delivers about 30%. A panel at 35° faces 55° up the sky, and gets about 87% in December and 95% in June. **At noon on the winter solstice a railing and a roof are nearly level; at the summer solstice the roof wins by a factor of three.**

The sky matters too. A vertical panel sees exactly half the sky dome, against about 91% for a panel at 35°, so it collects half the diffuse light a flat surface would. It also sees half the ground, and at the runs’ 0.20 reflectance that adds light equal to a tenth of what falls on the ground — a real contribution for a railing, under 2% for a panel at 35°. None of this makes a vertical panel a mistake. A railing is often the only surface a renter can use, and whether a bracket is allowed at all is a question for the building, not the model.

## Why a south railing is a winter panel

The same geometry flips the seasons. On a vertical south railing, **48 of the 51 cities make more electricity from December to February than from June to August** — a median of 1.84 times as much — and June is the weakest month of the year in 48 of them. Tilt the same panel to 35° and the pattern reverses: only Honolulu makes more in winter, and December is the weakest month in 41 cities.

New York shows the shape. An unshaded vertical south panel there makes 69 kWh in January and 30 in June. At 35° the same panel makes 97 in July and 57 in December.

The three exceptions are informative. In Anchorage, at 61°N, the December noon sun clears the horizon by barely 5°, so a railing makes about a third as much in winter as in summer. In Seattle and Portland, Oregon, the winter weather does the damage: a vertical south panel makes 101–108 kWh from December to February there, against 226 in Minneapolis and 187 in Billings at about the same latitude.

Two winter effects sit partly outside these runs. They fix ground reflectance at 0.20 all year and allow 1% of losses for snow, so they neither credit the extra light a snow-covered street or roof bounces up nor charge for a heavy fall that sits on the panel. For snowy cities, treat the winter months as approximate in both directions.

Two things stand out. First, ranking by railing is not the same as ranking by roof: the two orders have a rank correlation of only 0.54, because a vertical panel rewards clear, low-sun winters and a tilted one rewards high summer sun. Minneapolis is 8th for a railing and 31st at 35°; Manchester, New Hampshire, 17th and 44th; Houston 47th and 24th; Honolulu 51st and 9th. A rooftop solar map is a poor guide to a railing. Second, latitude alone predicts little: on a railing Minneapolis, at 45°N, out-produces every city in the Southeast, and Cheyenne outranks Phoenix.

## Ceilings, not expectations: shade, and New York

Every figure on this page assumes the panel sees an open sky. Real balconies rarely do. The building across the street, the balcony slab above, a street tree, a neighbor’s air conditioner: none of them are in these runs, and in a dense city they can remove a large share of the year — most of all in winter, when the low sun that suits a railing is also the sun most easily blocked. [Does my balcony get enough sun?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight) explains why obstruction and floor height can matter more than direction, and [how to calculate your balcony’s output](https://balco.nyc/calculate-balcony-solar-output) walks through applying them. The [calculator](https://balco.nyc/) takes any US address and a description of what stands opposite, and runs the same model with the shade included. A single year will also differ from these typical-year figures; PVWatts shows an expected range around each result, based on 30 years of weather.

New York City is the useful local check. For a point at City Hall, the unshaded runs put a vertical railing at **604 kWh a year facing south**, 562–567 facing south-west or south-east, 421–446 facing west or east and 167 facing north; a 60° bracket reaches 872 and 35° reaches 988. For a New York address the calculator also builds a 3D model of the surrounding buildings, which takes those ceilings down to what a particular floor and wall actually see.

New York ranks 43rd of 51 for a south railing, which is why the city’s case rests on [the price of a kWh](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate) rather than on its sun. Whether a few hundred kWh a year justifies a kit where you live is the subject of [whether balcony solar is worth it](https://balco.nyc/is-balcony-solar-worth-it).

## Common questions

**How many kWh does an 800 W balcony solar system produce per year?**

Hung vertically on an unshaded south-facing railing, about 660 kWh a year in the median US state's largest city, according to balco.nyc's PVWatts runs for all 51: from 510 kWh in Honolulu to 819 kWh in Albuquerque. Facing east or west it makes about 74% of that, facing north about 29%, and on a 35-degree bracket about 159%. Shade from nearby buildings reduces all of these figures.

**How much does an east-facing balcony solar panel produce?**

An 800 W panel hung vertically on an unshaded east-facing railing makes about 74% of what a south-facing one would, roughly 490 kWh a year in the median US state's largest city; the middle 80% of cities fall between 70% and 82%. West-facing is almost the same. In balco.nyc's PVWatts runs, west beat east in 13 of the 51 cities and east beat west in the rest, usually by a few percent.

**How much does a north-facing balcony solar panel produce?**

About 29% of a south-facing panel in the median US city, or roughly 200 kWh a year for an 800 W system on an unshaded vertical railing; balco.nyc's runs range from 149 kWh in Seattle to 241 kWh in Sioux Falls. It is not zero because a vertical panel sees half the sky whichever way it faces, and in summer the sun rises and sets north of due east and due west.

**How much more does a tilted balcony panel produce than a vertical one?**

Across balco.nyc's PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state, tilting a south-facing 800 W panel from vertical to 35 degrees raises annual output by a median of 59%; a 60-degree bracket adds 42% and 70 degrees 29%. The gain is smallest far north (33% in Anchorage) and largest near the tropics (85% in Houston, 129% in Honolulu), because a high summer sun strikes a vertical panel at a glancing angle.

**Does a balcony solar panel produce more in winter or summer?**

On a vertical south-facing railing, usually winter. In 48 of the 51 US cities balco.nyc modeled, an unshaded vertical south panel makes more from December to February than from June to August, a median of 1.84 times as much, because the low winter sun meets a vertical panel nearly head-on. The exceptions are Anchorage, Seattle and Portland, Oregon. A panel tilted to 35 degrees does the reverse and produces most in summer.

**Which state gets the most from a balcony solar panel?**

For an unshaded vertical south-facing railing, New Mexico, Nevada, Wyoming and Colorado lead: Albuquerque, Las Vegas, Cheyenne and Denver each make just over 800 kWh a year from 800 W in balco.nyc's PVWatts runs. Seattle, Portland (Oregon), Anchorage and Honolulu come last, at 510 to 535 kWh. Output is only part of the economics: what a kWh costs locally decides what that output is worth.

**How much does an 800 W balcony system produce in New York City?**

Unshaded, a vertical south-facing railing at New York's City Hall makes about 604 kWh a year in balco.nyc's PVWatts run; east or west 421 to 446, north 167, and a south panel on a 35-degree bracket 988. Buildings opposite reduce those figures; for a specific New York address the calculator models them in 3D.

## Sources

- [National Laboratory of the Rockies — PVWatts V8 API documentation](https://developer.nlr.gov/docs/solar/pvwatts/v8/): the model behind all 561 runs: tilt and azimuth inputs, albedo and monthly soiling, ac_annual and ac_monthly outputs in kWh, and 2020 TMY weather from the NSRDB.
- [PVWatts Calculator](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/): the public interface to the same model, for reproducing any figure here.
- [PVWatts Calculator — results and expected range](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/pvwatts.php): that PVWatts gives an expected range around each result based on 30 years of weather, since a single year differs from the typical year.
- [U.S. Department of Energy — Energy Department Renames NREL “National Lab of the Rockies” (1 December 2025)](https://www.energy.gov/cmei/articles/energy-department-renames-nrel-national-lab-rockies): the renaming of NREL.
- [U.S. Census Bureau — Vintage 2025 subcounty population estimates (SUB-EST2025)](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2020-2025/cities/totals/sub-est2025.csv): the largest city in each state and DC by July 2025 population, which sets the 51 locations.
- [EIA — 2024 Average Monthly Bill, Residential (Table 5A)](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/sales_revenue_price/pdf/table_5A.pdf): average residential consumption by state, from 495 kWh a month in Hawaii to 1,202 in Louisiana, behind the 4–12% share figures.
- [PVEducation — Elevation angle](https://www.pveducation.org/pvcdrom/properties-of-sunlight/elevation-angle): the solar-noon elevation from latitude and declination behind the 26° and 73° figures, and that between the equator and the Tropic of Cancer the summer noon sun comes from the north.
- [Sandia PV Performance Modeling Collaborative — Isotropic sky diffuse model](https://pvpmc.sandia.gov/modeling-guide/1-weather-design-inputs/plane-of-array-poa-irradiance/calculating-poa-irradiance/poa-sky-diffuse/isotropic-sky-diffuse-model/): the (1 + cos tilt)/2 sky view factor: half the sky dome for a vertical panel, about 91% at 35°.
- [Sandia PV Performance Modeling Collaborative — Ground-reflected irradiance](https://pvpmc.sandia.gov/modeling-guide/1-weather-design-inputs/plane-of-array-poa-irradiance/calculating-poa-irradiance/poa-ground-reflected/): the albedo × (1 − cos tilt)/2 ground term: a vertical panel sees half the ground.

# Condo, co-op and HOA rules: do solar-access laws cover balcony solar?

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-condo-hoa  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Rarely. balco.nyc read ten state solar-access statutes against a plug-in panel clamped to a condo or co-op balcony railing: one clearly covers it (Vermont, and only since a July 2026 amendment), two are unclear and seven do not. Most protect roofs or the owner’s own property and leave associations in control of common elements, which is where condo balconies commonly sit. Of the nine plug-in solar laws enacted so far, balco.nyc’s state tracker finds three that curb association bans (New Jersey, Vermont and, from 2027, Colorado), one that expressly preserves them (Virginia) and five that say nothing.

## Why solar-access laws mostly stop at the balcony

Solar-access laws, sometimes called solar-rights laws, are old and were written for one situation: a homeowner who wants panels on the roof of a house they own, and an association that wants to stop it. Florida’s dates from 1980. DSIRE, the state-policy database run by the NC Clean Energy Technology Center, counts solar access or easement laws in **45 states plus DC** as of March 2026, but that figure combines two different things. Easement statutes only let neighbors record an agreement not to block sunlight. Access statutes void association rules. Only the second kind helps with a board.

Three things in an access statute decide whether a railing panel is inside it:

- **What it protects.** Most define the device broadly enough to include a plug-in panel. New York’s does not: it covers only a system “installed on a rooftop”.

- **Where it applies.** Most protect installations on the owner’s own property, then give the association express control of the common elements.

- **Whom it binds.** Most name homeowners’ and condominium associations. Few mention co-ops.

The second point sinks most balcony claims. In a condominium you own your unit plus a share of everything else, and the balcony, its slab and its railing are commonly a *limited common element*: owned in common, reserved for your use. California makes that the default. Unless the declaration says otherwise, balconies and patios outside a unit are “exclusive use common area” (Civil Code §4145). Colorado’s 2026 plug-in law writes of a “limited common element patio, deck, or balcony”. A statute that protects the owner’s property and leaves common elements to the association therefore protects the roof of a house, not the railing of a condo. A co-op is further removed. The corporation owns the building and you hold shares and a proprietary lease, so there is no real property of yours for a statute to protect.

If you own a house or townhouse under an HOA and the deck is part of your own lot, several of these laws do reach it, subject to “reasonable” restrictions. This page is mainly about condos and co-ops, where the answer is mostly no.

> **Not legal advice.** This page summarizes statutes as written on 23 September 2026. Your declaration, bylaws or proprietary lease, and how your state’s courts read them, decide your case.

## Ten statutes, read against a railing panel

balco.nyc read the current text of each statute and asked one question: would a plug-in panel clamped to the railing of a condo or co-op balcony plausibly fall inside it? For each we noted how the statute defines the protected system, where it says the protection applies, and what it leaves to the association. “Unclear” means the text can reasonably be read either way. We did not survey case law, so a court in your state may already have settled a point we mark as open.

| State and statute | What it protects | Where it stops | A railing panel in a condo or co-op? |
|---|---|---|---|
| California, Civil Code §§714, 714.1, 4746 | Any “solar energy system”, defined broadly enough to include a plug-in panel. Governing-document rules that “effectively prohibit or restrict” one are void. A decision must be in writing, and an application not denied within 45 days is deemed approved. | In common areas the association may limit installations to “those systems approved by the association”. A balcony is common area unless the declaration says otherwise. The firmest protections (§714.1(b), §4746) are written for roofs. Stock cooperatives are covered. | Partly. The panel is inside the statute and the approval rules apply, but on the balcony the association keeps the power to approve. |
| Florida, §163.04 | Solar collectors and “other energy devices based on renewable resources”. Permission may not be denied “within the boundaries of a condominium unit”. | “This section shall not apply to patio railings in condominiums, cooperatives, or apartments.” | No for a railing mount. A panel standing inside the unit’s legal boundary is a closer question. |
| Texas, Property Code §202.010 | Any “solar energy device”. The chapter’s definitions include condominium regimes. | An association may prohibit a device on property it owns or maintains, on property owned in common, or anywhere on the owner’s property except the roof or a fenced yard or patio. | No. |
| Arizona, A.R.S. §§33-1816, 33-439 | A “solar energy device”, defined to include one serving a “multifamily structure”. Planned-community HOAs may not prohibit one. Covenants that “effectively prohibit” one are void. | §33-1816 excludes condominiums, leaving condo owners only §33-439, which says nothing about common elements. Arizona has no plug-in law, so utility rules still apply. | Unclear for condos. More plausible in a planned-community HOA. |
| Colorado, C.R.S. 38-30-168 | Covenants that restrict a “renewable energy generation device” are void. Reasonable aesthetic limits are allowed. | Confers no right to place a device on “a limited common element or general common element”. | No, today. From 1 January 2027 the plug-in law overrides this for limited common elements (section 3). |
| North Carolina, G.S. 22B-20 | Solar collectors on “residential property”. | “Residential property” excludes a condominium “in a multi-story building containing units having horizontal boundaries”. Covenants may also ban collectors visible from the ground on a facade facing common or public areas. | No. |
| Virginia, Code §55.1-1951.1 (condos), §55.1-1820.1 (HOAs) | A “solar energy collection device” on “that owner’s property”. | Protected only “unless the recorded declaration” prohibits it. The association “may prohibit or restrict” devices on common elements. | No. |
| Maryland, Real Property §2-119 | A “solar collector system” on “the roof or exterior walls” the owner owns or has exclusive use of. Condo bylaws and rules are covered. | An association “may prohibit or restrict” installation in common elements. | Unlikely. A railing is neither roof nor wall, and is usually a common element. |
| New York, Real Property Law §342 | A “solar power system”, defined as one “installed on a rooftop”, against HOA rules. | Associations may ban systems on property they own or members own in common. Condos and co-ops are not mentioned. | No. A railing is not a rooftop. |
| Vermont, 27 V.S.A. §544, amended by Act 149 | Solar collectors and, since 1 July 2026, plug-in devices “appurtenant to buildings”. Covenants may not prohibit them. | The old carve-out for “patio railings in condominiums, cooperatives, or apartments” now ends “except for a plug-in photovoltaic device”. | Yes, for a device that meets the Act’s definition (section 3). |

The tally is **one yes, two unclear and seven that do not** (or, in Maryland’s case, almost certainly do not). The one yes is recent and deliberate. Florida and Vermont had the same railing carve-out, word for word. Vermont amended its version in 2026 to except plug-in devices; Florida has not. Where a statute is silent about balconies the usual pattern decides it: protection for the owner’s property, association control of the common elements.

## The plug-in laws that reach associations

The new plug-in solar laws are mostly about the utility: they stop it requiring approval or an interconnection agreement for a small device. balco.nyc’s state tracker counts nine enacted as of 23 September 2026. Five — [Utah](https://balco.nyc/states/utah), [Maine](https://balco.nyc/states/maine), Maryland, [Connecticut](https://balco.nyc/states/connecticut) and [New Hampshire](https://balco.nyc/states/new-hampshire) — say nothing about associations. Maine comes closest. A customer who installs on “a structure the customer does not own” must protect its integrity and restore it on removal, which fits a condo balcony exactly but gives no right to use one. The other four go in different directions:

- **[New Jersey](https://balco.nyc/states/new-jersey)** (P.L.2026, c.82, signed 1 September 2026, effective 1 March 2027). Homeowners’ associations, condominium associations and cooperative housing corporations may not enforce governing documents that bar an owner or tenant from placing a device on the exterior of their premises. They keep “reasonable restrictions concerning the size, placement, or manner of placement of a portable solar generation device on the exterior of a unit owner’s or tenant’s premises”, and contrary provisions of a master deed or bylaws are void. Residents give 14 days’ written notice.

- **Vermont** (Act 149, in force 1 July 2026). The covenant rule in the table above now reaches railings, but only for a device that meets the Act’s definition: certified to UL 3700 “or an equivalent certification”, on a smart-metered supply, and “temporarily but securely attached”. As of September 2026 no complete plug-in system has been certified to UL 3700, so which products qualify is for now an open question.

- **Colorado** (HB26-1007; the association clauses apply from 1 January 2027). A covenant that “unreasonably” prohibits a device is void, and an owner “may install, use, or operate a device on real property that is a limited common element”. The association may require the device to be reasonably secured “to their unit or any limited common element patio, deck, or balcony”, and may put liability, costs and indemnity on the owner. It is the most balcony-specific text in any US statute we have read. Its express permission covers limited common elements, not general ones.

- **Virginia** (Chapters 1052 and 998, from 1 January 2027). The section that stops towns banning the devices says: “Nothing in this section shall be construed to supersede or limit” condominium instruments, the cooperative instruments of a co-op, or a property owners’ association declaration. Tenants of landlords with more than four units get a right to install. Condo owners do not, and a tenant renting a condo unit can be approved by the landlord and still refused by the association.

Both bills awaiting a governor are silent on associations. New York’s SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature. California’s SB 868 was presented to Governor Newsom on 31 August, with a 30 September deadline. Two bills that would have limited association rules died in 2026: [Oregon](https://balco.nyc/states/oregon)’s HB 4080 and [South Carolina](https://balco.nyc/states/south-carolina)’s H 4579. [Hawaii](https://balco.nyc/states/hawaii)’s condo-only SB 2902 also died, and would not have overridden association rules anyway.

**What the new right is worth.** balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs for each state’s largest city put an unshaded, south-facing 800 W railing system, after the site’s 0.95 railing factor, at 676.6 × 0.95 = **643 kWh** a year in Newark, 658 in Burlington and 805 in Denver. At each state’s EIA average residential price over the 12 months to June 2026 (23.81¢, 23.65¢ and 16.45¢), that is roughly **$153, $156 and $132** a year. Those are ceilings, not expectations: no shade, the best orientation, and state averages that include fixed charges and so overstate what a saved kWh is worth. The value of these laws is less the money than that they turn a flat no into a negotiation about placement.

## Co-ops, condos and New York City

For a New York City apartment none of section 2 helps. The state’s solar-rights statute, Real Property Law §342 (enacted in August 2021), covers rooftop systems and homeowners’ associations and mentions neither condos nor co-ops. The [SUNNY Act](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act), which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, would remove the utility barrier and nothing else. Its text says nothing about landlords, associations, co-ops or leases. In New York City, permission is entirely the board’s to give.

**Co-ops are not HOAs.** A co-op is a corporation that owns the building. You own shares and hold a proprietary lease, and the lease and house rules typically require the board’s written consent for alterations. Expect the request to become an alteration agreement. A condo is closer to an HOA. A board of managers administers the declaration and bylaws, and the balcony is often a limited common element, so a railing mount is a change to property you do not own alone.

**Courts defer to the board.** New York reviews co-op and condo board decisions under the business judgment rule set out in *Levandusky v. One Fifth Avenue Apartment Corp.* (1990). A decision made in good faith, within the board’s authority and for the building’s purposes will generally stand. Later cases carve out decisions with no legitimate relationship to the building’s welfare, or ones that single out an individual. There is no statute for a shareholder to invoke against a refusal.

**Why the board cares.** Owners of buildings over six stories must have their exterior walls and “appurtenances” inspected every five years under the city’s Façade Inspection & Safety Program. The rule’s list of appurtenances includes “railings” and “any equipment attached to or protruding from the facade”. A panel clamped to a railing plausibly falls into the second category. The building’s inspector would then have to examine it, and if it came loose it would be the building’s problem. Landmarked buildings add Landmarks Preservation Commission review. The practical detail is on [how to install balcony solar](https://balco.nyc/install-balcony-solar).

## How to ask a board

Where a statute does not decide it, which is most places, the board does. A vague request invites a vague refusal, so answer the board’s questions before it asks them:

- **Read your documents first.** Condo owners need the declaration, bylaws and rules. Co-op shareholders need the proprietary lease and house rules. Look for clauses on alterations, the exterior, terraces and anything attached to railings. In New Jersey, Vermont, Colorado or California, quote the specific statute text above. In New York, do not lead with the law, because there is none on your side.

- **One page on the hardware.** Name the product and its certification listing, the panel’s size and weight, and how it attaches. The strongest answers are inside the railing, clamped rather than drilled, with a secondary tether. Say which outlet the cable reaches and by what route, and how the whole thing comes down.

- **Offer the paperwork.** Offer an alteration agreement with an indemnity, and a certificate of insurance. California’s rule for systems on a shared condo roof is a usable model: liability coverage kept in force, with a certificate within 14 days of approval and every year after (§4746). Commit to removal and restoration at your own cost on sale, on request, and for facade inspections or repairs.

- **An engineer’s letter if asked.** The install guide recommends one anyway for glass or aged railings. Weigh its cost against the money at stake. balco.nyc’s New York City band is 400 to 900 kWh a year for an 800 W system, roughly $136 to $306 at Con Edison’s 34¢ marginal rate. Conditions costing more than a year or two of that change the decision. [The calculator](https://balco.nyc/) gives the figure for your own balcony.

- **Time the request.** In New York you can ask for approval conditional on the SUNNY Act taking effect, since the utility barrier stays until it does. In Colorado and New Jersey, the dates in section 3 change what a board is allowed to refuse.

- **Get the answer in writing**, including any conditions, and keep it with your lease or deed.

If the board says no in a state without a plug-in association clause, that is usually the end of it. A floor-standing panel that attaches to nothing still needs an outdoor outlet and still falls under the building’s rules. It is a better request, not a way around the board. If the answer is a firm no, [renters’ options](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-renters) and [the state laws side by side](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared) show what may change and when.

## Common questions

**Can my HOA or condo association ban solar panels on my balcony?**

In most states, yes, if the balcony is a common element, which it commonly is in a condominium. Solar-access laws generally protect roofs or the owner's own property and let associations prohibit or restrict devices on common elements. The exceptions for plug-in panels are Vermont (since 1 July 2026), New Jersey (from 1 March 2027) and Colorado (from 1 January 2027), where associations may set reasonable limits on placement but may not simply ban the devices. This is a summary of statutes, not legal advice.

**Does my state's solar access law protect a balcony solar panel?**

Usually not for a condo or co-op balcony. balco.nyc read ten state statutes (California, Florida, Texas, Arizona, Colorado, North Carolina, Virginia, Maryland, New York and Vermont) against a railing-mounted plug-in panel: only Vermont's clearly covers it, California's and Arizona's are unclear, and the other seven either exclude condo railings, protect only roofs, or let associations control common elements. Florida's statute says outright that it does not apply to patio railings in condominiums, cooperatives or apartments.

**Can a New York City co-op board refuse balcony solar?**

Yes. New York's solar-rights statute, Real Property Law section 342, covers only rooftop systems and homeowners' associations and does not mention co-ops, and the SUNNY Act, which awaits the Governor's signature, would give no right to install. Co-op alterations are governed by the proprietary lease and house rules, and New York courts review board decisions under the business judgment rule, so a refusal made in good faith and within the board's authority will generally stand.

**Does the SUNNY Act let me install balcony solar in my co-op or condo?**

No. The SUNNY Act (S8512C / A9111C) has passed both chambers of the New York Legislature and awaits the Governor's signature. It would exempt small plug-in devices from utility interconnection and approval, but its text says nothing about landlords, associations, co-ops or leases, so board permission would still be required.

**Which states stop condo associations from banning plug-in solar?**

As of 23 September 2026, three: Vermont, whose covenant rule has covered qualifying plug-in devices on condo, co-op and apartment patio railings since 1 July 2026; New Jersey, where associations may not enforce bans on exterior placement from 1 March 2027; and Colorado, where from 1 January 2027 an owner may install a device on a limited common element such as a balcony. Virginia's law expressly does not override condominium, co-op or HOA documents, and the other five enacted plug-in laws are silent on associations.

**What should I give my board when asking to install balcony solar?**

A one-page description of the product and its certification, its size and weight, how it attaches (ideally inside the railing, clamped not drilled, with a secondary tether), which outlet it uses and how it is removed. Offer an alteration agreement with an indemnity, a certificate of liability insurance, and a commitment to remove it and restore the railing at your own cost on sale, on request or for facade work. Get the answer and any conditions in writing.

# What does a balcony solar kit cost in NYC?

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-04

balco.nyc uses hardware-only cost assumptions of $850 budget, $1,200 mid-range, and $1,600 premium for a typical 800-watt system. These are planning benchmarks, not currently verified New York offers. At Con Edison’s $0.34 per kilowatt-hour, a well-sited system saves roughly $300 a year and pays back in three to five years. A shaded, low-floor balcony takes six to ten.

## What a kit costs right now

balco.nyc models a typical 800 W New York City setup at three hardware-only price points: **$850 budget**, **$1,200 mid**, and **$1,600 premium**. Treat these as planning benchmarks rather than currently verified New York offers. They cover panels, a microinverter, cabling, and a railing mount — not an electrician or building work.

Per watt, those assumptions are **$1.06**, **$1.50**, and **$2.00**. Because system cost and output both scale roughly with size, siting usually changes payback more than kit size does.

For a current price reference, Bright Saver lists **180 W at $285.30** and **360 W at $414.17** for members, plus a $29 annual membership. The non-member prices are **$499** and **$699**. As of September 2026, Bright Saver says it cannot ship these kits to New York because no system on the market yet has the whole-system certification New York requires.

We cite Bright Saver as a transparent US hardware-price benchmark, not as a kit New Yorkers can currently order. balco.nyc does not rank brands, take affiliate revenue, or tell you what to buy.

> **Prices and availability changed quickly in 2026. Check the seller’s current price, certification, and New York shipping status before budgeting.**

## The costs that are not the kit

The kit price is the part that is easy to look up, which is why most coverage stops there. Budget for the rest before you decide:

- **An outlet.** A plug-in system needs a weather-rated outlet on the balcony. Many NYC balconies do not have one. Adding one is a licensed-electrician job, often through an exterior wall, sometimes requiring building permission. We have no reliable price for this in NYC and will not guess — get two quotes before you buy a kit. On a balcony with no outlet this can be a large fraction of the kit price.

- **Mounting.** Included brackets suit common railing profiles. Glass balustrades, thick concrete parapets and unusual rail geometry may need something else.

- **Permission.** Co-op boards, condo boards and landlords may say no, or say yes with conditions on the mount, the colour, or the visibility from the street. That costs time, and occasionally a more expensive mount.

- **Membership or shipping**, where a seller charges them.

- **Replacement.** Panels and microinverters are usually warranted for different lengths of time. Check both before assuming a 25-year life.

These are excluded from the payback table below. Add yours to the kit cost column and re-read it.

## What a kilowatt-hour is actually worth to you

balco.nyc values avoided consumption at **$0.34/kWh** — Con Edison SC-1 all-in marginal cost, supply plus delivery plus surcharges. It is the number that changes when you use one less kilowatt-hour, and [why we use it rather than a supply-only figure](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate) is a page of its own.

Your bill also carries a fixed monthly customer charge. **Solar does not touch it.** It is excluded from the $0.34 marginal rate, and in the worst siting case it is larger than everything the panels save you. Your bill will not go to zero.

The bigger point, and the one most coverage of balcony solar gets wrong: **there is no net metering for these devices.** The SUNNY Act exempts them from interconnection and net-metering requirements, which cuts both ways — no utility approval, and no credit for export. A kilowatt-hour your panels make while your apartment is drawing less than they produce goes to the grid and earns you **nothing**.

So every saving figure below is a *ceiling*: it assumes every kilowatt-hour generated displaces one you would otherwise have bought. Multiply by whatever share you actually self-consume. As arithmetic rather than as a balco.nyc estimate: if a fifth of your generation were exported, a $187 year-one saving becomes about $150, and a 6.0-year payback becomes about 7.4 years.

## The payback arithmetic, worked

An 800 W system in New York City produces roughly **400–900 kWh a year**. The spread across balconies is about **3×** from worst to best — high floor facing south against low floor facing north, with the buildings across the street doing most of the damage.

The table runs four production levels across the band. Savings are year one at $0.34/kWh, at 100% self-consumption. Payback years account for 3%/year rate escalation and 0.5%/year panel degradation, and are the year cumulative savings first exceed the kit price.

| Annual output | Year-1 saving (ceiling) | Payback, $850 kit | Payback, $1,200 kit | Payback, $1,600 kit | 25-yr net, $1,200 kit (nominal) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 400 kWh (poorly sited) | $136 | 5.9 yr | 8.1 yr | 10.4 yr | +$3,435 |
| 550 kWh | $187 | 4.4 yr | 6.0 yr | 7.9 yr | +$5,175 |
| 700 kWh | $238 | 3.5 yr | 4.8 yr | 6.3 yr | +$6,915 |
| 900 kWh (well sited) | $306 | 2.7 yr | 3.8 yr | 5.0 yr | +$9,235 |

Read across a row rather than down a column. Moving from the premium kit to the budget kit at fixed siting saves you about four and a half years in the worst row. Moving from the worst siting to the best at a fixed kit saves you four to five. **Where the panel points matters about as much as what you pay for it, and you can only change one of those after you have signed the lease.**

## How to read the 25-year number

The last column is in **nominal dollars, not discounted to present value**. This matters more than it sounds. Nominal totals are the standard way this gets reported and they systematically flatter the result.

Take the 550 kWh row. Twenty-five years of escalating, degrading output totals about **$6,375** nominal. Discount that stream at 3% a year and it is worth about **$4,277** in today’s money. Net of a $1,200 kit: **+$5,175 nominal, +$3,077 in present value**. Same panels, same sun, a third less money once you account for the fact that a dollar in 2051 is not a dollar now.

Two other assumptions sit inside that number. Rate escalation is set at **3%/year** by default, with 2% and 4% presets — at 2% the totals fall noticeably and paybacks stretch, and this is a forecast, not a measurement. Panel degradation is **0.5%/year** on the mid tier, so year-25 output is about 88% of year one.

And the model itself carries a stated accuracy of **±15%**, widening to ±20% where it falls back to coarser irradiance data. That is a modelled band, *not field-validated* — nobody has yet put instrumented kits on a representative sample of New York balconies. A 6.0-year payback should be read as roughly 5.2 to 7.1 years. See [methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology) for how the band is derived.

## When the answer is no

If your balcony is on a low floor, faces north, or spends the middle of the day in the shadow of the building opposite, the arithmetic is bad and you should not spend the money on economic grounds.

Work it through. Roughly 400 kWh a year is **$136** of avoided electricity at best. Put that against a $1,600 premium kit and payback is **10.4 years** before you add an electrician, before you subtract exported kilowatt-hours you are not paid for, and before the ±15% band, which could push it past 12. If you may move within five years, and you probably will if you rent, you will not get your money back.

Buy the cheapest kit that is properly certified, or do not buy one. A budget kit on a poor balcony pays back in 5.9 years; a premium kit on the same balcony takes 10.4. Paying more for a system that will never see full sun is the single most expensive mistake available here.

> **None of this is legal in New York yet.** The SUNNY Act passed both chambers in late May 2026 and awaits the Governor’s signature; it takes effect 90 days after signing. Do not buy hardware on the assumption the timeline will hold — see [the SUNNY Act status page](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act).

Run your own floor, orientation and consumption through [the calculator](https://balco.nyc/) rather than reading a row off this table. The table is four points on a wide band; your balcony is one point.

## Common questions

**How much does a balcony solar kit cost in NYC?**

For a typical 800 W setup, balco.nyc uses hardware-only planning assumptions of $850 at the budget end, $1,200 mid-range, and $1,600 premium. As of September 2026, Bright Saver lists a 360 W kit at $414.17 for members, plus a $29 annual membership, and $699 without membership, but says it cannot ship the kit to New York because no system on the market yet has the whole-system certification New York requires. None of these figures include an electrician or building work.

**Is balcony solar worth it in New York?**

It depends almost entirely on your balcony, not on the kit. A high-floor, south-facing, unshaded balcony producing 900 kWh a year saves about $306 and pays back a mid-range kit in 3.8 years. A low-floor, north-facing one producing 400 kWh saves $136 and takes 8.1 years on the same kit — or over 10 on a premium one, which is a bad deal.

**Do I get paid for the electricity I don't use?**

No. The SUNNY Act exempts these devices from net metering, so any kilowatt-hour you generate and do not consume at that moment goes to the grid uncompensated. This is the most important fact about the economics and most coverage gets it wrong. Every saving figure on this page assumes full self-consumption and is therefore a ceiling, not an expectation.

**What is the payback period for balcony solar in NYC?**

Between roughly 2.7 and 10.4 years, depending on siting and kit price, assuming full self-consumption. A mid-range $1,200 kit lands between 3.8 and 8.1 years across the typical 400–900 kWh production band. Those figures include 3%/year rate escalation and 0.5%/year panel degradation, and carry a modelled plus or minus 15% accuracy band.

**Will balcony solar zero out my Con Edison bill?**

No. Con Edison charges a fixed monthly service charge that does not change with how much you generate. On a poorly sited balcony that fixed charge alone can exceed the entire annual saving. Solar only reduces the variable portion of the bill, which balco.nyc values at $0.34 per kilowatt-hour.

**Should I buy the premium kit?**

On a well-sited balcony the difference is about 1.2 years of payback and defensible. On a poorly sited one it is 4.5 years and hard to justify. Since output is set by your floor, orientation and shading rather than by kit quality, paying up for hardware that will never see full sun is the most expensive error available. balco.nyc does not recommend specific products or brands.

## Sources

- [Bright Saver — balcony solar kits](https://www.brightsaver.org/balcony-solar-kits): current member and non-member prices, plus Bright Saver’s notice that it cannot ship to New York because no market system yet has the required whole-system certification.
- [Bright Saver begins offering plug-in solar kits at wholesale costs nationwide (13 July 2026)](https://pv-magazine-usa.com/2026/07/13/bright-saver-begins-offering-plug-in-solar-kits-at-wholesale-costs-to-customers-nationwide/): reports the July 2026 launch and price pairs; the seller’s current page is the source for present New York availability.
- [A new deal on balcony solar just dropped in the US (July 2026)](https://www.canarymedia.com/articles/solar/balcony-panel-bright-saver-deal): effective prices of $1.75/W and $1.23/W once the annual membership is included.
- [SUNNY Act passes the NYS Legislature](https://www.nysenate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2026/liz-krueger/sunny-act-passes-nys-legislature-bringing-plug-solar-one): passage of S8512C / A9111C through both chambers.
- [Balcony solar plug-in power awaits Hochul's signature](https://www.newyorkalmanack.com/2026/07/balcony-solar-plug-in-power-hochul/): the bill unsigned as of July 2026, with a year-end deadline and a 90-day commencement.
- [Will New York Gov. Kathy Hochul sign a balcony solar bill?](https://www.canarymedia.com/articles/solar/new-york-gov-sign-balcony-solar-bill): the exemption from interconnection and net-metering requirements, and what it implies for export credit.

# The balcony solar kWh formula: estimate output by hand

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-kwh-formula  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

For a panel on a balcony railing, multiply its watts by your state’s vertical-south yield (0.67 to 1.08 kWh per watt a year), a direction factor (0.74 for east, 0.29 for north), 0.95 for the railing and a shade factor. Tested against balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state, that formula lands within 3.5% of the full simulation in the median case. The familiar rooftop formula, kW × peak sun hours × 365 × performance ratio, overstates a south-facing railing by about 60% and an east- or west-facing one more than twofold.

## The rooftop formula, and why it overstates a railing

The formula that circulates for estimating solar output by hand is **kWh a year = system kW × peak sun hours × 365 × performance ratio**. A peak sun hour is one kilowatt-hour of sunlight per square meter, so a place receiving 4.5 kWh/m² a day has 4.5 peak sun hours. The performance ratio covers inverter, wiring, heat and dirt losses; consumer guides quote 0.75 to 0.85, and the original PVWatts used an overall derate of 0.77.

On a roof, the formula works. balco.nyc took NREL’s latitude-tilt solar resource for the largest city in each state (the Solar Resource API, which returns no data for Anchorage, so 50 places) and set the formula against its own PVWatts runs for an 800 W panel tilted 35° to the south. With a performance ratio of 0.75 the formula came within **2.4%** of PVWatts in the median city; at 0.80 it ran 6.6% high.

On a railing, it does not. In Chicago NREL gives 4.50 peak sun hours at latitude tilt, so 0.8 kW × 4.50 × 365 × 0.75 = **986 kWh**. PVWatts puts the same panel on a 35° south roof at 1,010 kWh: close. Hung vertically on a south-facing railing, with the 5% railing loss the site applies to every vertical estimate, it makes **616 kWh**. The formula is 60% high. Across the 50 places the median overstatement for a south-facing railing is **61%**, and it grows as the railing turns away from south: the formula gives about 2.2 times the real output facing east or west, and about 5.5 times facing north. It has no term for direction at all.

The arithmetic is fine; the input is wrong. A peak-sun-hour figure describes sunlight on a horizontal or latitude-tilted surface, and many published tables do not say which. A railing panel is neither. It faces the horizon, so the high summer sun strikes it at a glancing angle; it sees half of the sky’s diffuse light, where a 35° panel sees about nine-tenths; and more of its direct light arrives at steep angles, where the glass reflects it away, a loss PVWatts models explicitly. In balco.nyc’s runs a vertical south panel, after the railing loss, makes a median **62%** of what the same panel makes at 35°, from 43% in Honolulu to 74% in Anchorage. Using horizontal peak sun hours instead does not rescue the formula: at the same 0.75 performance ratio it still overstates a south railing by a median 39%.

## A formula built for a railing

balco.nyc’s balcony formula keeps the shape of the rooftop one, but every input describes a vertical panel:

> **kWh a year ≈ W × Ystate × Fdir × (1 − 0.05) × Sshade**

| Term | What it is | Typical value | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|---|
| W | The panels’ rated power in watts | 400 or 800 | The label |
| Ystate | kWh a year per watt from a vertical, south-facing panel with an open view, before the railing loss | 0.67 to 1.08; median 0.87 | balco.nyc’s PVWatts run for the state’s largest city (section 3) |
| Fdir | Output in your direction as a fraction of south | 1.00 S, 0.93–0.96 SE/SW, 0.73–0.74 E/W, 0.29 N | Median across 51 cities (section 4) |
| 1 − 0.05 | Railing loss: the rail, brackets and the slab above clip the panel’s lower edge | 0.95 | The factor the calculator applies to every vertical panel (methodology) |
| Sshade | The share of that light the buildings opposite let through | 1.00 for an open view; 0.18–0.94 in a street canyon | balco.nyc’s street-canyon model (section 5) |

A worked example: an 800 W system on an east-facing 10th-floor balcony in Chicago, looking across the street at a building of six to ten stories. That building is lower than the balcony, so nothing is blocked and S is 1.00.

**800 × 0.81 × 0.74 × 0.95 × 1.00 ≈ 456 kWh a year.**

PVWatts, run for an east-facing vertical panel in Chicago and given the same railing loss, says 444 kWh. The hand calculation is 2.5% high. Now move the same system to a south-facing 2nd-floor balcony, 20 meters from that same building. Direction improves, to 1.00; shade collapses, to 0.31:

**800 × 0.81 × 1.00 × 0.95 × 0.31 ≈ 191 kWh a year.**

The better-facing balcony makes less than half as much. In a city, your floor and what stands opposite usually move the answer more than the compass does.

## Ystate: the number that depends on where you live

Y is the input that depends on where you live. balco.nyc ran NREL’s PVWatts V8 for an 800 W vertical south-facing panel at the largest city in every state and DC, with the calculator’s own parameters, and divided the annual output by 800. Half the states fall between 0.81 and 0.94 kWh per watt a year. A selection:

| Largest city | Ystate (kWh per W a year, before railing loss) | 800 W, vertical south, open view, after railing loss |
|---|---|---|
| Albuquerque | 1.08 | 819 kWh |
| Denver | 1.06 | 805 kWh |
| Phoenix | 1.02 | 778 kWh |
| Minneapolis | 0.96 | 730 kWh |
| Los Angeles | 0.95 | 720 kWh |
| Boston | 0.89 | 673 kWh |
| Median of 51 | 0.87 | 658 kWh |
| Chicago | 0.81 | 616 kWh |
| Jacksonville | 0.80 | 612 kWh |
| New York City | 0.79 | 604 kWh |
| Houston | 0.76 | 576 kWh |
| Seattle | 0.69 | 524 kWh |
| Honolulu | 0.67 | 510 kWh |

Every state is on [the state pages](https://balco.nyc/states), which carry the same runs. The order is not the order of a rooftop sunshine map, and that is the second reason the rooftop formula misleads. Ranked by what a 35° roof panel produces, Minneapolis is 31st of the 51 cities; ranked by what a vertical railing produces, it is 8th. Jacksonville falls from 13th to 40th, Houston from 24th to 47th, and Honolulu from 9th to last. A wall-mounted panel likes a low sun, which strikes it nearly square on in a northern winter, while near the tropics the sun spends much of the year high overhead and passes over the panel’s face. Across the 51 cities, the ratio of vertical to 35° output rises steadily with latitude (a correlation of 0.90).

Each Y comes from one city. The runs do not measure variation inside a state, which in a large or mountainous state can be substantial; the [calculator](https://balco.nyc/) runs PVWatts for your exact address.

## Fdir: which way the railing faces

F is output in a given direction divided by output facing south, from the same PVWatts runs. The medians across the 51 cities, and how far individual cities stray from them:

| Railing faces | Fdir (median) | Middle half of cities | Full range |
|---|---|---|---|
| South | 1.00 | — | — |
| South-west | 0.96 | 0.93–0.98 | 0.91 (Billings) to 1.13 (Honolulu) |
| South-east | 0.93 | 0.92–0.96 | 0.87 (Anchorage) to 1.11 (Honolulu) |
| East | 0.74 | 0.72–0.79 | 0.61 (Anchorage) to 1.07 (Honolulu) |
| West | 0.73 | 0.70–0.77 | 0.66 (Billings) to 1.05 (Honolulu) |
| North-east | 0.46 | 0.44–0.49 | 0.41 (Anchorage) to 0.73 (Honolulu) |
| North-west | 0.44 | 0.42–0.47 | 0.39 (Denver) to 0.70 (Honolulu) |
| North | 0.29 | 0.29–0.32 | 0.25 (Albuquerque) to 0.42 (Honolulu) |

The pairs are close enough to share a number (about 0.95, 0.74 and 0.45); pairing them moves the test results in section 6 by a few tenths of a point. The medians also sit close to the fixed factors in the calculator’s New York fallback model (0.92, 0.72, 0.45, 0.32), which were set independently.

The factors drift with latitude in the same way Y does. Near the Gulf, where the summer sun is high, a south wall loses more and east and west lose less: east is 0.88 of south in Houston and New Orleans and 0.86 in Jacksonville, well above the 0.74 median. In Honolulu the order inverts, and east and west both out-produce south. In Anchorage east is only 0.61. If you are in Hawaii, skip the direction factor and use [the Hawaii page](https://balco.nyc/states/hawaii), which has the run for each direction.

## Sshade: what stands across the street

With an open view (a park, water, or buildings lower than your floor) S is 1.00, at every orientation, because PVWatts has already priced direction. Otherwise S depends on how tall the obstruction is, how far away, and how high you are.

balco.nyc’s street-canyon model treats the building opposite as a continuous wall parallel to your facade and traces the sun against it through the year. These figures come from the calculator’s own code, run for a south-facing balcony in Chicago (41.88°N), 20 meters across a street, with a balcony height of (floor − 1) × 3.05 m + 1.0 m:

| Across the street (20 m away) | 2nd floor | 5th floor | 10th floor |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nothing, an open view | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| 1 to 2 floors, or trees (7 m) | 0.94 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| 3 to 5 floors (13 m) | 0.75 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| 6 to 10 floors (25 m) | 0.31 | 0.58 | 1.00 |
| 11 floors or more (43 m) | 0.18 | 0.24 | 0.47 |

These are the factors as the calculator applies them: monthly, to monthly output, here weighted by Chicago’s vertical-south PVWatts months. The model’s one-line annual summary, weighted by New York’s monthly sunshine, reads higher under heavy shade: 0.40 rather than 0.31 on the 2nd floor opposite six to ten stories, 0.63 rather than 0.58 on the 5th, 0.55 rather than 0.47 on the 10th opposite a tower. The gap is seasonal. A south railing does its best work in winter (in Chicago, 65 kWh in January against 35 in June), exactly when the low sun sits behind the building opposite. Use the lower figures.

Three cautions. An east- or west-facing balcony loses more to the same building, because its direct sun arrives low: 0.64 rather than 0.75 on the 2nd floor opposite three to five stories. The same street blocks more sun further north, less further south. And a continuous wall has no gaps, so it errs toward too much shade. What it cannot see at all (a tree, an air-conditioner, the slab overhead) is covered in [how much sun a balcony gets](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight).

## How wrong the formula is

balco.nyc tested each version against the PVWatts run it tries to predict, both with the 5% railing loss applied. The state-yield test leaves out south, since Y is built from the south run and would score zero by construction: seven directions in 51 places, 357 predictions. The national-yield test keeps all eight directions (408), and the rooftop tests use a south railing in the 50 places with NREL sun-hour data, or all 51 for the calibrated version.

| Version | Median error | 1 prediction in 10 is off by more than | Worst case |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rooftop formula, NREL peak sun hours, performance ratio 0.75, south railing | +61% | +88% | +157% (Honolulu) |
| Rooftop formula calibrated exactly to each city’s 35° roof, south railing | +61% | +82% | +132% (Honolulu) |
| Balcony formula with one national Y (0.87), all 8 directions | 5.5% | 19% | +50% (Anchorage, east) |
| Balcony formula with each state’s Y, 7 non-south directions | 3.5% | 12% | −37% (Honolulu, north-east) |
| The same, leaving out Honolulu | 3.4% | 10% | +22% (Anchorage, east) |

The rooftop formula overstated every railing it was tested on. Even calibrated perfectly to each city’s own roof, with peak sun hours times performance ratio taken straight from the 35° PVWatts run, it is 61% high. That isolates the cost of going vertical: no choice of derate fixes it.

The balcony formula with state yields lands within 10% of PVWatts in 87% of cases. Its large misses cluster where section 4 says they will. Every Honolulu direction is under-predicted, by 15% to 37%; the Gulf-state cities (Houston, New Orleans, Jackson and Jacksonville) are under-predicted in most directions away from south, by up to 21%; and Anchorage facing east is over-predicted by 22%. Those five states and Alaska account for 28 of the 46 predictions that miss by more than 10%. Using one national Y instead roughly doubles the share of predictions off by more than 10%, from one in eight to one in four; for a south railing it overstates Seattle and Portland, Oregon, by 25% and understates Albuquerque by 20%. That is what location is worth.

These are errors against a model, not a meter. PVWatts has its own uncertainty, and balco.nyc’s stated accuracy for its fullest New York estimates is a modeled band of about 15%, not a field-validated one. A hand result is no better than PVWatts; round it to the nearest 25 kWh.

## What a hand formula cannot see

Five multiplications cannot carry everything a year of simulation does:

- **The seasons.** One annual number hides that a south railing is winter-heavy and an east or west one summer-heavy, which matters on a seasonal rate.

- **The interactions.** The terms are multiplied as if independent; in fact shade depends on direction and season, and direction factors on latitude.

- **Your street.** Y is one city per state; S assumes one uniform building opposite.

- **Money and permission.** kWh is not savings: value it at [your marginal rate](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate), remembering that the state averages used outside New York City include fixed charges. Whether you may install a plug-in system varies by state and building; nothing here is legal advice.

Used for what it is, the formula answers the first question well: is this a 600 kWh balcony or a 200 kWh one? For a figure to act on, the [calculator](https://balco.nyc/) runs PVWatts for your exact address, applies shade month by month, and in New York City uses the real buildings around you.

## Common questions

**What is the formula for balcony solar panel output?**

balco.nyc's hand formula for a railing-mounted panel is: kWh a year ≈ watts × Y × F × 0.95 × S. Y is the vertical-south yield for your state (0.67 to 1.08 kWh per watt a year across the largest city in each state, median 0.87), F is the direction factor (1.00 south, about 0.95 south-east or south-west, 0.74 east or west, 0.29 north), 0.95 is the railing loss and S is the shade factor (1.00 for an open view). Tested against PVWatts in all 51 places, it came within 3.5% in the median case.

**Can I use peak sun hours to estimate a balcony panel's output?**

Not directly. Peak sun hour figures describe sunlight on a horizontal or latitude-tilted surface, and a vertical railing panel receives much less. Using NREL's latitude-tilt figures and a 0.75 performance ratio, the standard formula (kW × peak sun hours × 365 × performance ratio) overstated a south-facing railing by a median 61% in balco.nyc's comparison across 50 states, and an east- or west-facing one by more than double.

**How much does an 800 W balcony solar system produce a year?**

Mounted vertically on a south-facing railing with an open view, balco.nyc's PVWatts runs put it at 510 to 819 kWh a year after a 5% railing loss, from Honolulu to Albuquerque, with a median of about 658 kWh across the largest city in each state. Facing east or west, multiply by about 0.74; facing north, by about 0.29; then multiply by a shade factor if taller buildings stand opposite.

**Why does a vertical solar panel produce less than a tilted one?**

A vertical panel faces the horizon, so the high summer sun strikes it at a glancing angle, it sees only half of the sky's diffuse light, and more of its direct light arrives at steep angles where the glass reflects it. Across the largest city in each state, a vertical south-facing panel with a 5% railing loss produced a median 62% of what the same panel tilted at 35 degrees produced, from 43% in Honolulu to 74% in Anchorage.

**Does an east- or west-facing balcony work for solar?**

It produces about three-quarters of what a south-facing one does: a median factor of 0.74 for east and 0.73 for west across the largest city in every state, in balco.nyc's PVWatts runs. Near the tropics east and west do relatively better, because the sun spends much of the year high overhead: in Houston and New Orleans east is about 0.88 of south, and in Honolulu east and west both out-produce south.

**How accurate is a hand calculation of balcony solar output?**

Accurate enough to tell a 600 kWh balcony from a 200 kWh one. Against PVWatts, balco.nyc's balcony formula errs by 3.5% in the median case and by more than 10% about one time in eight, mostly in Hawaii, Alaska and the Gulf states. PVWatts is itself a model rather than a meter, so a hand result is best rounded to the nearest 25 kWh.

## Sources

- [NREL — PVWatts V8 API documentation](https://developer.nlr.gov/docs/solar/pvwatts/v8/): the model behind every run on this page: NSRDB typical-year weather, tilt and azimuth inputs (180° = south), and ac_annual / ac_monthly as annual and monthly AC output in kWh.
- [NREL — Solar Resource Data API documentation](https://developer.nlr.gov/docs/solar/solar-resource-v1/): the latitude-tilt and horizontal daily solar resource (kWh/m²/day, i.e. peak sun hours) used for the rooftop-formula test; the API returned no data for Anchorage.
- [NREL — PVWatts Version 5 Manual (Dobos, 2014)](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/downloads/pvwattsv5.pdf): the Perez plane-of-array model, the angle-of-incidence reflection correction, the 14% default system losses, and the 0.77 overall derate of the original PVWatts.
- [U.S. DOE OSTI — Performance Parameters for Grid-Connected PV Systems (Marion et al., 2005)](https://www.osti.gov/biblio/15016389): performance ratio and reference yield as the standard parameters relating PV output to the solar resource.
- [SolarReviews — Peak sun hours explained](https://www.solarreviews.com/blog/peak-sun-hours-explained): the definition of a peak sun hour as an hour at 1,000 W/m², and an example of a state table that does not say which surface it describes.
- [NREL — PVWatts Calculator](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/): where any figure on this page can be re-run for a specific address, tilt and azimuth.
- [U.S. Census Bureau — Vintage 2025 subcounty population estimates](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2020-2025/cities/totals/sub-est2025.csv): the source for the largest city in each state, which is the reference point for every state run.
