# What the US plug-in solar laws actually say, provision by provision

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Nine US states have signed plug-in solar laws, and five are in force today: Utah, Maine, Colorado, Maryland and Vermont. All nine stop the utility from requiring its approval and eight cap a device at 1,200 W, but only four limit what a landlord, association or town can do, and the certification wording differs enough that a kit can qualify in one state and not the next. balco.nyc’s compilation of the legislature pages, weighted by Census population, puts 5.2% of US residents under a law in force today, and 29.5% if every signed law and the New York and California bills take effect.

## The count on 23 September 2026

balco.nyc checked plug-in solar legislation in all 50 states and the District of Columbia on 23 September 2026, from each legislature’s own bill pages and enacted text rather than third-party trackers, which disagree with the primary sources on several effective dates. (Trackers list Maryland’s as taking effect on signing or on 1 October; the act and the state’s fiscal note both say 1 July 2026.) The result:

| Status | Count | Where | Share of US residents |
|---|---|---|---|
| In force | 5 | Utah, Maine, Colorado, Maryland, Vermont | 5.2% |
| Signed, not yet in force | 4 | Connecticut (1 Oct 2026), Virginia and New Hampshire (1 Jan 2027), New Jersey (1 Mar 2027) | 6.9% |
| Passed, awaiting a governor | 2 | New York, California | 17.4% |
| Bill pending | 7 | District of Columbia, Illinois, Massachusetts, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania | 19.6% |
| Bill died, 2025–26 | 18 | Alaska, Arizona, Delaware, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Oregon, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Washington, West Virginia, Wyoming | 21.7% |
| No bill found | 15 | Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, North Dakota, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Wisconsin | 29.3% |

The shares are balco.nyc’s arithmetic: each jurisdiction’s July 2025 Census Bureau population estimate, summed by status, over the 341.8 million total for the 50 states and DC (rounded). Read cumulatively, **5.2% of US residents** live where a plug-in law is in force today, 12.1% will once New Jersey’s starts on 1 March 2027, and 29.5% would if New York and California enact theirs. Sources for every state are on [the states page](https://balco.nyc/states).

> **No law is not the same as a ban.** Before its act passed, Maryland’s legislative analysts noted that balcony solar was not prohibited there, but that utilities “frequently require customers to enter into interconnection agreements” first. That is broadly the position in the 42 jurisdictions without a signed law. A plug-in law takes the device out of that process.

## “Exempt from interconnection” is not a right to install

Every plug-in law can answer two separate questions. Most answer only the first.

**The utility question** is whether you need your power company’s permission. A device that feeds power into your wiring while the grid is live is, in utility rules, a small generator, which normally needs an interconnection application and agreement before it runs. All nine signed laws bar the utility from requiring its approval, charging a fee or demanding extra equipment; eight expressly free the device from interconnection agreements or review, and Colorado gets there by listing what the utility may not demand. That is “exempt from interconnection”, and it is the whole of what Utah, Maine, Maryland, Connecticut and New Hampshire do.

**The property question** is whether anyone else can stop you: a landlord, a lease, a condominium declaration, a homeowners’ association, a town’s zoning. An interconnection exemption does not touch any of it. A *right to install* is a separate clause that makes some of those prohibitions unenforceable, usually while allowing “reasonable” limits on size and placement. Only Vermont, Virginia, New Jersey and Colorado have one.

Two points get lost in between. **Notice is not approval**: Maryland and Virginia require notice to the utility before installing, Maine within 30 days above 420 W, and none lets the utility refuse a compliant device. And **codes still apply**: Connecticut says its exemption does not reach the building and fire codes or “any local ordinance or regulation”, and Colorado and New Jersey require installation to meet the fire, electrical or construction codes.

## The utility side, law by law

The first matrix is what each enacted text says about the device and the utility, quoting the statute where the wording matters. “Not addressed” means we read the provision and it is silent; “unclear” means it says something that does not settle the point. NRTL is a nationally recognized testing laboratory; NEC the National Electrical Code. The two bills awaiting a governor are in italics; they are not law.

| Law | In force | Size cap, as worded | Certification wording | Utility notice | Net metering and exports |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| UtahHB 340 | 7 May 2025 | 1,200 W “maximum power output”; AC or DC not stated | “Certified by Underwriters Laboratories or an equivalent” NRTL; NEC | None | “Not subject to” net metering |
| MaineLD 1730 | 29 Jul 2026 | 1,200 W AC inverter output per address; above 420 W, licensed electrician and dedicated circuit | “In accordance with UL 3700”, a comparable NRTL standard, or configured per the NEC | Within 30 days, above 420 W only | “May not be used for net energy billing” |
| ColoradoHB26-1007 | 12 Aug 2026; property rules 1 Jan 2027 | 1,920 W “to the electric grid”; one system per address | “Labeled and listed” by an NRTL; from 2027, over 391 W must be “UL labeled and listed” to be sold | Utility may ask for presence and size | Not addressed |
| MarylandHB 1532 | 1 Jul 2026 | 1,200 W supplied back to the building; one per meter | “Certified by Underwriters Laboratory or an equivalent” NRTL | Before installing, with a safety and capacity certification | Outside net metering; no renewable energy credits |
| VermontAct 149 | 1 Jul 2026 | 1,200 W combined inverter capacity per meter; smart meter required | “Complies with UL 3700” or an equivalent certification; IEEE 1547 | None | Ineligible; exports “shall not be compensated” |
| ConnecticutPA 26-127 | 1 Oct 2026 | 1,200 W “maximum power output”; one per meter | UL or an equivalent NRTL, “and meets” UL 1741; IEEE 1547; NEC | None | Must warn that excess is “charged to the customer as usage” without a net-metering meter |
| VirginiaHB 395 / SB 250 | 1 Jan 2027 | 1,200 W per customer or multifamily unit | An NRTL (29 CFR 1910.7) or equivalent; NEC | State form before installing; utility has 15 days to query it | Outside net metering |
| New HampshireSB 540 | 1 Jan 2027 | 1,200 W AC inverter output; one per metered customer | An NRTL, to “nationally recognized safety standards” (none named) | Optional, after installation | Unclear: no credit provided |
| New JerseyS2368 / A4836 | 1 Mar 2027 | 1,200 W combined per address or dwelling unit | “In accordance with” UL 3700 or “a comparable standard”, by an NRTL | None | Outside net-metering requirements; credit not addressed |
| New YorkSUNNY Act (bill) | 90 days after enactment | 1,200 W AC inverter nameplate, to the grid | NRTL listing “as a complete plug-in photovoltaic system” | Within 30 days | “Uncompensated” unless the owner opts in |
| CaliforniaSB 868 (bill) | 1 Jan 2027 if enacted; exemption ends 2030 | 1,200 W aggregated AC per dwelling | “Certified as a plug-in photovoltaic system” by UL or an NRTL | Utility may require online registration | Not addressed |

The caps do not all measure the same thing. Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire and California’s bill cap inverter AC output, so panel wattage behind a smaller inverter does not count; Maryland, Colorado and New York’s bill cap what is supplied back to the building or grid; Utah, Connecticut and New Jersey say only “maximum power output”. Several also limit the number of devices: one per meter in Maryland, Connecticut and New Hampshire, one system per address in Colorado.

## The property side: landlords, associations and towns

The second matrix is where the laws genuinely diverge. Five of the nine say nothing about who else may stop you; four do, each in its own way.

| Law | Landlord and tenant | HOA, condo and co-op | Local government |
|---|---|---|---|
| Utah | Not addressed | Not addressed | Not addressed |
| Maine | No right; on a structure you do not own you must protect it, meet building, fire and zoning codes, and restore it | Not addressed | Not addressed |
| Colorado | From 2027, no “unreasonable” prohibition; the owner may set reasonable limits, including prior notice | From 2027, unreasonable covenants are void; may install on a limited common element such as a balcony | Fire and local building codes apply; the 2027 bar binds any “person”, which includes governments (our reading) |
| Maryland | Not addressed | Not addressed | Not addressed in §7-321 |
| Vermont | 10 days’ notice; the landlord may set reasonable restrictions; silence lets the tenant proceed | Covenants may not prohibit, including on condo, co-op and apartment patio railings | Zoning bylaws may not regulate them |
| Connecticut | Not addressed | Not addressed | Local ordinances and codes still apply |
| Virginia | Landlords with more than four units may not prohibit on the tenant’s exterior; reasonable limits; 7 days’ notice | Not overridden: association, condo and co-op instruments preserved | May not prohibit on residential structures; height, setback and historic rules apply |
| New Hampshire | Not addressed | Not addressed | Not addressed |
| New Jersey | May not bar tenants who pay their own electric bill, including on a balcony or patio; reasonable limits; 14 days’ notice | May not enforce bans on exterior placement; reasonable limits allowed | May not prohibit, or require a permit, fee or approval |
| New York (bill) | Not addressed | Not addressed | Not addressed |
| California (bill) | Not addressed | Not addressed | Not addressed |

The four rights are not one right. Vermont’s turns on notice: silence from the landlord lets the tenant proceed. Virginia’s covers only tenants of landlords with more than four units, and leaves condominium and association documents intact. New Jersey’s covers tenants who pay their own electric bill and also binds associations and towns. Colorado’s bars “unreasonable” prohibitions from 1 January 2027; our reading that it reaches towns rests on state law defining a “person” to include governmental subdivisions.

On balco.nyc’s population arithmetic those four states hold **7.3%** of US residents, but three of the four rights are not yet operative. The only one in force today is Vermont’s, covering about 0.2%. What this means in practice is covered in [balcony solar for renters](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-renters) and [condos, co-ops and HOAs](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-condo-hoa).

## Why a kit that qualifies in one state may not qualify in the next

Each law protects only a device that meets its own definition, and the definitions differ most in the certification clause:

- **Certified by a lab, standard unnamed:** Utah, Maryland, Virginia and Colorado. None says certified *to what*, or whether listings of the separate components count.

- **A component standard, or a description of one:** Connecticut adds UL 1741, the inverter standard; New Hampshire asks for “nationally recognized safety standards” without naming one.

- **UL 3700 or something comparable:** Maine, Vermont and New Jersey. Maine and New Jersey identify UL 3700 by its title, an “Outline of Investigation”, and Maine also accepts a system configured to the electrical code.

- **Certified as a complete system:** New York’s bill and California’s.

The spread matters because, as of September 2026, no complete plug-in system has been certified to UL 3700; the components (panels, microinverters) carry their own listings. A kit sold with a UL 1741-listed microinverter and listed panels may therefore satisfy the unnamed-standard wording of Utah or Maryland, while in Vermont the question becomes what counts as an “equivalent certification”, and under New York’s or California’s bill whether any complete-system listing exists for it at all. The statutes do not answer those questions and we cannot either. The standard itself is covered in [what UL 3700 is, and is not](https://balco.nyc/ul-3700-plug-in-solar-certification), and the hazards these clauses target in [is plug-in solar safe?](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe)

Certification is not the only trap. A device sized to Colorado’s 1,920 W cap falls outside every other state’s definition. An 800 W kit that meets Utah’s definition with no installer requirement needs, in Maine, a licensed electrician and a dedicated circuit. Vermont allows devices only on smart-metered services. And a second unit behind the same meter in Connecticut or Maryland takes you outside the law even if each unit qualifies.

## The patterns: 1,200 W, 391 W, and exports nobody pays for

**1,200 W is the default.** Of the 36 jurisdictions where balco.nyc found a plug-in bill in 2025–26, 34 wrote in a wattage figure, and 30 of those chose 1,200 W, including eight of the nine signed laws and both bills now with a governor. The exceptions: Colorado’s 1,920 W, also proposed by [New Mexico](https://balco.nyc/states/new-mexico)’s SB 157 before it died; [Delaware](https://balco.nyc/states/delaware)’s 800 W bill; and Illinois. Utah’s 2025 law, the first, is visibly the template: Connecticut, Virginia and New Jersey reuse its definition almost word for word, down to “intended primarily to offset part of the customer’s electricity consumption”.

**391 W is the other number.** Colorado, Maryland and Virginia exempt devices at or below 391 W from code or listing provisions that would require rewiring; New Jersey sets that line at 400 W, and Maine’s unconditional tier stops at 420 W. None of the texts explains 391, and we could not trace its origin. [Illinois’](https://balco.nyc/states/illinois) SB 3104, as amended in committee in March 2026, would make it a ceiling: it prohibits any system above 391 W until the National Electrical Code adopts a standard for them, about a third of what every signed law allows. It cleared committee 9–4, was sent back to the Assignments committee on 22 May 2026, and has not moved since.

**Exports are almost never paid for.** Six of the nine signed laws expressly take the device out of net metering (Utah, Maine, Maryland, Vermont, Virginia, New Jersey), and none provides another credit. Vermont says exports “shall not be compensated”; Connecticut goes further, requiring a warning that excess generation is charged as usage unless the meter allows net metering. Colorado is silent, and New Hampshire shields the utility from “compensation or charges” without saying more. The one bill in balco.nyc’s data that would have credited exports, [Oregon](https://balco.nyc/states/oregon)’s HB 4080, died in March 2026. See [why surplus earns nothing](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering).

**Who is bound varies by utility.** The statutes bind utilities under different labels (“electrical corporation”, “electric company”, “electric distribution company”, “electric public utility”, “provider of retail electric service”), each defined by its own state’s law. California’s bill names local publicly owned utilities outright; most others leave it to those definitions, which we have not resolved state by state. If you buy power from a municipal utility or a cooperative, ask it whether the law applies.

## The two bills on a governor’s desk, and checking your own state

[New York](https://balco.nyc/states/new-york)’s SUNNY Act (S8512C / A9111C) has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature. The final version cleared both on 28 May 2026; as of 23 September the Assembly’s record shows no delivery to the Governor, so her decision clock has not started. If signed, it takes effect on the 90th day. It would exempt devices of up to 1,200 W AC from interconnection and net metering, leave exports uncompensated unless the owner opts into an agreement, require notice within 30 days, and require listing as a complete system. It grants no right to install: renters, co-op shareholders and condo owners would still need permission. [The SUNNY Act in detail](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act).

[California](https://balco.nyc/states/california)’s SB 868 was presented to Governor Newsom on 31 August 2026. Under the state constitution he has until 30 September to act, or it becomes law without his signature; if enacted, it takes effect on 1 January 2027. It binds local publicly owned utilities as well as investor-owned ones, and is silent on exports, landlords and associations. It is the only text here with an end date: the exemption is repealed on 1 January 2030, the day a ban begins on selling plug-in devices that do not meet its code and certification conditions.

For any state, check five things against the enacted text before relying on a summary, including this one: the effective date; how the cap is measured; the certification wording, against your device’s paperwork; whether and when the utility must be told; and whether the law mentions your landlord, association or town — if it does not, their rules still apply. This page summarizes statutes as written. It is not legal advice, and a utility, court or building department may read a clause differently.

## Common questions

**Which states allow plug-in or balcony solar?**

As of 23 September 2026, nine states have signed plug-in solar laws. Five are in force: Utah, Maine, Colorado, Maryland and Vermont. Connecticut's takes effect on 1 October 2026, Virginia's and New Hampshire's on 1 January 2027, and New Jersey's on 1 March 2027. New York's SUNNY Act and California's SB 868 have passed both chambers and await their governors. Elsewhere a plug-in system is not necessarily banned, but the utility's ordinary interconnection rules for generators apply.

**Which states give renters a right to install balcony solar?**

Four signed laws limit a landlord's power to say no, each differently. Vermont lets a tenant proceed if the landlord does not answer a 10-day notice; Virginia bars landlords with more than four units from prohibiting devices on the exterior of the tenant's premises; New Jersey protects tenants who pay their own electric bill; Colorado bars unreasonable prohibitions. Only Vermont's is in force today: Colorado's and Virginia's start on 1 January 2027 and New Jersey's on 1 March 2027. Utah, Maine, Maryland, Connecticut and New Hampshire give tenants no such right, and neither would New York's SUNNY Act.

**Is 1,200 watts the limit in every state?**

Nearly. Eight of the nine signed plug-in solar laws cap devices at 1,200 W, and 30 of the 34 jurisdictions whose 2025-26 plug-in bills set a wattage figure chose 1,200 W. Colorado allows 1,920 W supplied to the grid. Maine allows up to 420 W with no conditions and up to 1,200 W only if a licensed electrician installs each system on a dedicated circuit and the utility is notified. The caps are also measured differently: some count inverter AC output, some the power supplied back to the building or grid, and some just say maximum power output.

**Do plug-in solar laws pay you for electricity sent to the grid?**

Almost never. Six of the nine signed laws take plug-in devices out of net metering and none provides another credit; Vermont's says exported power shall not be compensated, and Connecticut's requires a warning that excess generation will be charged as usage unless the meter allows net metering. New York's SUNNY Act would leave exports uncompensated unless the owner opts into an agreement. Plan on the value coming only from electricity you use yourself.

**What does 'exempt from interconnection' mean for plug-in solar?**

It means the utility cannot make you apply, sign an interconnection agreement, pay a fee or add equipment before using a compliant device, as it can for a rooftop array. It says nothing about whether a landlord, condo board, homeowners' association or town can stop you; that takes a separate right-to-install clause, which only four of the nine signed plug-in laws (Vermont, Virginia, New Jersey and Colorado) contain.

**If a plug-in solar kit is legal in one state, is it legal in another?**

Not necessarily. Each law protects only devices that meet its own definition, and the certification wording differs: Utah and Maryland ask for certification by UL or an equivalent lab without naming a standard, Maine, Vermont and New Jersey name UL 3700 or a comparable standard, and New York's and California's bills require certification as a complete plug-in system. As of September 2026 no complete plug-in system has been certified to UL 3700. Wattage caps, per-meter device limits and Vermont's smart-meter requirement also differ.

**Is balcony solar legal in New York or California yet?**

Not yet in either. New York's SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature; it had not been delivered to her as of 23 September 2026 and would take effect 90 days after becoming law. California's SB 868 was presented to Governor Newsom on 31 August 2026; he has until 30 September 2026 to act, it becomes law without his signature if he does not, and it would take effect on 1 January 2027.

# Balcony solar claims, checked: nine numbers traced to their source

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-myths  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Of nine claims widely repeated about balcony solar, one holds up roughly as stated, two are best cases presented as typical, and six are wrong or out of date. balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state and DC put an unshaded, south-facing 800 W railing system at a median 6.4% of the average home’s electricity (4.2% to 11.9%), not 15–25%, and at a median payback of 9.9 years on a $1,200 kit, with no state under four. The claim that survives is the unexpected one: a north-facing railing really does produce about 70% less than a south-facing one.

## The nine claims and their verdicts

Each claim below is stated as it usually circulates, traced as far back as we could take it, and checked against balco.nyc’s own data: NREL’s PVWatts V8 run with the calculator’s settings for an 800 W system at the **largest city in each of the 50 states and DC**; the EIA’s state prices and household consumption; and every state’s plug-in solar law, researched from legislature pages and checked on 23 September 2026.

|  | The claim | Where it comes from | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | An 800 W kit covers 15–25% of your electricity | Solar.com’s 2026 guide, among others; no derivation given | A ceiling. A south-facing railing panel covers a median 6.4% of the state-average home. No state reaches 15% |
| 2 | A north-facing balcony produces 75% less | Earliest we found: a 2024 newsletter. It matches a PVGIS run for a vertical panel in Berlin | Roughly right for an unshaded vertical panel: 58% to 75% less in US cities, median 71% |
| 3 | You need four hours of direct sun a day | Could not be traced | No threshold exists. A north-facing railing gets essentially no direct sun from October to March and still produces a median 70 kWh |
| 4 | It pays for itself in two years | Bright Saver, for a kit bought at cost in a high-rate state | A special case. A $1,200 kit on a south railing takes 4.8 to 13.9 years, median 9.9 |
| 5 | You get the 30% federal tax credit | IRC §25D, which was real through 2025 | Out of date. It ended for expenditures after 31 December 2025 |
| 6 | It keeps your lights on in a blackout | Could not be traced | False. The inverter must shut off within 2 seconds of an outage |
| 7 | Any outlet will do | Sellers’ shorthand for “it has a plug” | False. It needs a weather-rated outdoor outlet on a circuit with room for it |
| 8 | It is legal in every state | Seller copy | False. 5 states have a law in effect and 4 more have signed one |
| 9 | It sells your surplus back to the grid | Carried over from rooftop net metering | False under the signed laws. Six rule it out, three are silent, none provides a credit |

That is one claim that holds up roughly as stated (2), two best cases presented as typical (1 and 4), and six that are wrong or out of date. Every output figure on this page applies the site’s railing-obstruction factor — 0.95 for a vertical panel, 0.99 at 35° — and none includes shade from neighboring buildings, so each is the *unobstructed best case* for its city. Paybacks use the calculator’s own loop: 0.5% a year panel degradation, prices rising 3% a year, and every kilowatt-hour used at home at the state’s EIA average price.

## Output: 15–25%, 75% less, four hours of sun

### 1. “An 800 W kit covers 15–25% of your electricity”

Solar.com’s 2026 guide says a standard 800 W kit can often cover 15% to 25% of a typical apartment’s monthly electricity. It shows no working, and we found none elsewhere. balco.nyc’s runs give this:

| 800 W, facing south, unshaded | kWh a year (median city) | Share of the state’s average home | Share of an average large-building apartment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vertical, on a railing | 658 | 4.2% to 11.9%, median 6.4% | 8.4% to 13.4%, median 10.8% |
| Tilted to 35° | 1,053 | 7.3% to 21.3%, median 10.3% | 11.7% to 22.6%, median 17.3% |

Against the average home in its own state (EIA, 2024: a median of about 10,600 kWh a year), no state’s railing panel reaches 15%. Thirteen stay under 5%, most of them Southern states where homes use the most electricity; only California, Maine and New Mexico pass 10%. A fairer test of an apartment claim is an apartment: the EIA’s 2020 Residential Energy Consumption Survey puts households in buildings of five or more units at 20.8 million Btu of electricity, about **6,100 kWh a year**. A railing panel still tops out at 13.4% of that. The 15–25% only appears when the panel is tilted to 35°, sits in full sun and serves a smaller-than-average user — then 48 of the 51 land between 15% and 23%, and none reaches 25%. It is a ceiling, not an expectation. In New York City, balco.nyc’s 3D shade model puts real balconies at 400–900 kWh, 6% to 13% of the state-average home.

### 2. “A north-facing balcony produces 75% less”

The earliest instance of this figure we have found is a February 2024 newsletter post that states it, together with “30% less” for east and west, without showing the calculation; its listed sources include the European Commission’s PVGIS tool, run for Berlin. We reran PVGIS for Berlin ourselves with an 800 W vertical panel: **612 kWh facing south, 154 facing north — 74.8% less**. East and west averaged 419 kWh, 31.5% less. Both numbers match, so a Berlin PVGIS run is the likely origin, though we cannot confirm the author used exactly that.

The surprise is that it roughly survives the trip to America. balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs put a vertical north-facing railing **58% to 75% below** a south-facing one, with a median of 71%; 28 of the 51 cities lose 70% or more. The biggest losses are in the clear-skied Southwest — Albuquerque 75%, Las Vegas 75%, Phoenix 74% — because there the south side has the most direct sun to win. The smallest is Honolulu, 58%, where the midsummer sun passes north of overhead. So the verdict is roughly right, for an unobstructed vertical panel. What it leaves out is everything but the compass: in a street canyon a high-floor north balcony can out-produce a boxed-in south one, which is [why balco.nyc models the block rather than the direction](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight).

### 3. “You need four hours of direct sun a day”

The threshold circulates as four hours, four to five, or six to eight, and one guide we read gave two different figures on one page. We could not trace any version to a study or a standard. A panel has no threshold: it produces whatever the light allows, continuously. The cleanest test is a north-facing railing. Between the September and March equinoxes the sun rises and sets south of due east and west everywhere in the United States, so a north-facing vertical panel gets essentially *no* direct sun for half the year — zero hours, not four. balco.nyc’s runs still give it a median **70 kWh from October to March**, all of it from diffuse and reflected light, about 35% of its annual output. Small, and no reason on its own to buy, but proof that output fades with the light rather than switching off at a line. The useful question is how many kilowatt-hours, which [our guide to balcony sunlight](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight) works through.

## Money: the two-year payback and the tax credit

### 4. “It pays for itself in two years”

The most specific source we found is Bright Saver, a nonprofit that sells kits at cost. It says that in a sunny, high-rate state such as California or New York, a kit bought at its at-cost price typically pays back in about two years. Its price is the first condition: 360 W for $414.17 to members, about $1.15 a watt, against $1.50 a watt for balco.nyc’s $1,200 mid-range assumption for 800 W. Rerun on balco.nyc’s assumptions, a $1,200 kit on an unshaded south-facing railing pays back as follows:

| Payback on a $1,200 kit | States (of 51) | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Under 2 years | 0 | — |
| Under 4 years | 0 | — |
| 4 to 5 years | 1 | California (Los Angeles), 4.8 |
| 5 to 8 years | 12 | Hawaii 5.2, Massachusetts 5.5, New York 6.6 |
| 8 to 10 years | 15 | Pennsylvania 8.1, Colorado 8.3, Illinois 9.4 |
| 10 years or more | 23 | Florida 11.2, Texas 11.5, Louisiana 13.1; Washington (Seattle) slowest at 13.9 |

The median is **9.9 years**. The arithmetic for the fastest state: 720 kWh a year in Los Angeles at California’s average 32.89¢ is $237 in year one, and rising prices bring $1,200 back in 4.8 years. Even the $850 budget kit gets under five years in only eight states, all high-price ones: California, Hawaii and six in the Northeast. Two years does reproduce, but only when three conditions line up. Take Bright Saver’s 360 W price, tilt the panel to 35° instead of hanging it on a railing, and put it in Los Angeles: about 579 kWh (the 800 W run scaled to 360 W), $190 a year, **2.1 years**, or 2.3 counting the $29 membership. Hang the same panel on a railing and it is 3.8 years. At balco.nyc’s budget price, a tilted 800 W system beats two years in two states, Hawaii and California. A $1,200 kit on a railing does it nowhere. These figures are generous (section 6); the [cost and payback guide](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost) works the same arithmetic for New York City.

### 5. “You get the 30% federal tax credit”

This one was true. The residential clean energy credit under IRC §25D paid 30% of the cost of solar electric property installed from 2022 through 2025, and pages written in that period still say so. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21, signed 4 July 2025) ended it: the IRS says the credit is not allowed for any expenditure made after 31 December 2025, and that an expenditure counts as made when installation is complete. A kit installed in 2026 earns no federal credit, even one paid for in 2025. balco.nyc’s payback figures net out no credit. The details are in [our tax credit guide](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-tax-credit).

## Hardware: blackouts and outlets

### 6. “It keeps your lights on in a blackout”

It does the opposite, by design. Grid-connected inverters are built to IEEE Std 1547-2018 and tested under UL 1741. The standard requires them to detect an outage — an “unintentional island” — and stop energizing the line **within 2 seconds**, then wait, by default, five minutes after the grid returns before starting again. The reason is safety: a line crew must be able to treat a dead line as dead. State plug-in laws write the same rule in. Utah requires a feature that stops the device energizing the building during an outage; Maine requires inverters that shut off 0.2 seconds after power is disrupted. We could not trace the belief to any source. Our guess is that it comes from portable “solar generators”, battery units that do run appliances in an outage because they connect to nothing. Backup power from a balcony means a battery system, a separate product and a separate decision.

### 7. “Any outlet will do”

A plug-in kit does end in an ordinary plug. That is true of the plug, not of every outlet, and three things narrow it:

- **It has to be outdoors and rated for it.** An outlet on a balcony needs to be one rated and covered for a wet location, and many balconies have none. Adding one is work for a licensed electrician, and in an apartment building usually needs the building’s approval too; [the installation guide](https://balco.nyc/install-balcony-solar) lists what to check.

- **The circuit behind it matters.** A standard breaker does not see current that a plug-in panel injects into the circuit, so household load plus solar output can exceed what the wiring was designed for without tripping anything. Protection against overloads is one of the things UL Solutions’ certification program for plug-in systems tests for.

- **Some laws specify the outlet.** Maine lets a household run up to 420 W without an electrician, but anything larger, up to 1,200 W, must be installed by a licensed electrician on a dedicated circuit with a single outlet.

None of this is electrical advice: which outlet and circuit suit a given home is a question for an electrician.

## Law: every state, and selling power back

### 8. “It is legal in every state”

We saw this in the footer of one kit seller’s website in August 2026, on a page whose own article counted ten states with laws. balco.nyc has now reviewed all 50 states and DC from their legislatures’ bill pages. As of 23 September 2026:

| Status | Count | States |
|---|---|---|
| Law in effect | 5 | Colorado, Maine, Maryland, Utah, Vermont |
| Signed, not yet in effect | 4 | Connecticut (1 Oct 2026), New Hampshire (1 Jan 2027), Virginia (1 Jan 2027), New Jersey (1 Mar 2027) |
| Passed, awaiting signature | 2 | California (SB 868), New York (SUNNY Act) |
| Bill pending | 7 | DC, Illinois, Massachusetts, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania |
| Bill failed or vetoed | 18 | Alaska, Arizona, Delaware, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Oregon, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Washington, West Virginia, Wyoming |
| No plug-in law found | 15 | Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, North Dakota, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Wisconsin |

Where there is no law, plug-in solar is not banned as such, but the utility’s interconnection rules apply, and those usually require approval before anything feeds power into a home circuit. New York’s SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature; it would grant no right to install. California’s SB 868 was presented to Governor Newsom on 31 August 2026. Even where a law is in effect, most do not stop a landlord or a condo board from saying no: four of the nine signed laws (Colorado, New Jersey, Vermont, Virginia) limit that power in different ways, and the other five give no right to install. This is not legal advice; [every state’s bills, dates and limits](https://balco.nyc/states) are listed with their sources, and [the SUNNY Act page](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act) covers New York.

### 9. “It sells your surplus back to the grid”

Rooftop solar usually earns credit for exported power under net metering, and the assumption carries over. For plug-in systems it mostly does not. Of the nine signed laws, **six rule it out**: Utah and Maryland exempt the devices from net-metering rules, Maine bars them from net energy billing, Virginia excludes them from its definition of an eligible customer-generator, and Vermont says exported generation shall not be compensated. Connecticut goes further: its law requires a warning that surplus is charged to the customer as usage unless the meter allows net metering. Colorado, New Hampshire and New Jersey are silent. New York’s bill would leave exports uncompensated unless the owner signs a separate agreement, and California’s is silent. None provides a credit. balco.nyc therefore assumes surplus earns nothing in every state, which is why the share of output used at home — the fridge, the router, whatever runs in daylight — matters as much as the output itself.

## What these numbers leave out

The figures behind the nine verdicts are generous in some ways and blunt in others. Five limits are worth knowing before quoting them:

- **One city per state.** Each state is represented by its largest city. Buffalo is not New York City, and Flagstaff is not Phoenix. The [state pages](https://balco.nyc/states) name the city behind every number.

- **No shade.** Every output figure assumes nothing blocks the sky. In New York City balco.nyc’s 3D model finds roughly a threefold spread between the best and worst realistic balconies, mostly from the buildings opposite.

- **Average prices.** The EIA’s state averages divide total revenue by total sales, so they include fixed monthly charges a panel cannot touch. That overstates the value of a kilowatt-hour you avoid buying. In New York City the calculator uses Con Edison’s marginal rate of 34¢ instead, and anywhere else the per-kWh rate from your own bill is the better input.

- **Everything used at home.** Savings and paybacks assume every kilowatt-hour displaces one you would have bought. Surplus earns nothing (claim 9), so a home that exports part of its output saves less.

- **Modeled, not metered.** These are PVWatts simulations over a typical weather year, not measurements from installed systems.

The pattern across the nine claims is consistent: the numbers that travel furthest describe a tilted, unshaded panel serving a light user in a high-price state, then get repeated as if they described a railing panel anywhere. For one balcony rather than 51 cities, [run your own address](https://balco.nyc/); the [methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology) sets out every assumption used here.

## Common questions

**Is balcony solar a scam?**

No. A plug-in panel does generate electricity and cut a bill, but the most repeated numbers oversell it. balco.nyc's PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state put an unshaded, south-facing 800 W railing system at a median 658 kWh a year: about 6.4% of the average home's use, worth about $109 a year at the state's average price. It saves money slowly: balco.nyc's model finds no state where a $1,200 kit on a south-facing railing pays back in under four years.

**Does balcony solar really save money?**

Yes, but slowly in most states. On balco.nyc's $1,200 mid-range kit price, an unshaded south-facing 800 W railing system pays back in 4.8 years in California, the fastest, and 13.9 years in Washington, the slowest, with a median of 9.9 years across the 50 states and DC. Those figures assume every kWh is used at home and prices rise 3% a year; shade or unused surplus makes them longer.

**How much of my electricity will an 800 W balcony kit cover?**

For a south-facing railing panel, usually 4% to 12% of an average home's use, with a median of 6.4%, according to balco.nyc's PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state. The often-quoted 15-25% needs a panel tilted to about 35 degrees, no shading, and an apartment with below-average consumption.

**Does a north-facing balcony really produce 75% less?**

Close, for an unshaded vertical panel. balco.nyc's PVWatts runs put a north-facing railing 58% to 75% below a south-facing one across US cities, with a median of 71%, and the 75% figure matches a PVGIS calculation for a vertical panel in Berlin. In a dense city, the buildings opposite often matter more than the compass direction.

**Does balcony solar work during a power outage?**

No. Grid-connected inverters must detect an outage and stop energizing the line within 2 seconds under IEEE Std 1547-2018, and plug-in laws such as Utah's and Maine's require the same, so that line crews are not put at risk. Power during a blackout needs a battery system, which is a separate product.

**Is plug-in solar legal in every state?**

No. As of 23 September 2026, balco.nyc's review of all 50 states and DC finds a plug-in solar law in effect in 5 states (Colorado, Maine, Maryland, Utah, Vermont), signed but not yet in effect in 4 (Connecticut, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Virginia), and passed and awaiting signature in 2 (California, New York). Elsewhere the utility's interconnection rules apply, which usually means approval is required. This is not legal advice.

**Can I sell surplus balcony solar power back to the utility?**

Generally no. Six of the nine signed plug-in solar laws exclude these devices from net metering or deny any export credit, and the other three are silent; none provides a credit. Connecticut's law requires a warning that surplus is charged to the customer as usage unless the meter allows net metering.

**Can I still claim the 30% federal solar tax credit on a balcony kit?**

Not for a kit installed now. The residential clean energy credit under IRC section 25D ended for expenditures made after 31 December 2025 under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and the IRS treats an expenditure as made when installation is complete, so a kit installed in 2026 earns no federal credit.

---

# Do you get paid for balcony solar power you don’t use?

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-net-metering  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Almost certainly not. None of the nine state plug-in solar laws signed so far requires a utility to pay for power a balcony system sends back to the grid, five of them expressly shut these devices out of net metering, and New York’s SUNNY Act says exports “shall be uncompensated.” So the number that matters is how much you use yourself: balco.nyc’s hourly PVWatts run for an 800 W south-facing railing in New York City finds that an apartment drawing a steady 150 W uses about 60% of the output and gives the other 240 kWh a year away.

## Surplus power is given away, not sold

A plug-in panel’s power goes first to whatever the apartment is drawing at that moment: the fridge, the router, a laptop charger. Only when the panel produces more than the apartment uses does anything flow back out through the meter to the neighbors. That outflow is the surplus.

The arrangement that pays for exports is net metering, under which the kilowatt-hours you send out are credited against the ones you buy. Net metering normally comes with an interconnection application and utility approval — exactly the paperwork plug-in laws exempt these devices from. The trade the states have made is consistent: no application, no fee, no credit. This is not legal advice, and it varies by state and utility, but the safe planning assumption is that surplus earns **nothing**.

That makes one number decisive: the share of the panel’s output you use at the moment it is produced. balco.nyc’s calculator, like most, assumes that share is 100% and values every kWh at Con Edison’s all-in marginal rate of 34¢. That is a ceiling. To see how far below it a real apartment sits, balco.nyc ran NREL’s PVWatts V8 hour by hour for an 800 W system on a vertical, south-facing railing in New York City, with the calculator’s own parameters. The hourly run reproduces the 635.7 kWh a year in the site’s state data exactly; less the 5% railing loss the site applies to vertical panels (a factor of 0.95), that is about **604 kWh**. Set hour by hour against an apartment drawing a steady 150 W, 364 kWh of it is used at home and **240 kWh** leaves through the meter. At 34¢ that is a saving of about $124 a year, not the $205 the 100% assumption gives.

## What each plug-in law says about exported power

Nine states have signed plug-in solar laws, and bills in New York and California have passed their legislatures. balco.nyc read each in the legislature’s own text. Five expressly shut plug-in devices out of net metering, three say nothing about paying for exports, and Connecticut requires a warning that exports may be billed. None requires a utility to pay for them.

| State | Law | Status (23 Sep 2026) | What it says about exports |
|---|---|---|---|
| Utah | HB 340 (2025) | In force since 7 May 2025 | “Not subject to the net metering program requirements”; residential net metering now starts above 1,200 W. Unpaid. |
| Maryland | HB 1532, ch. 353 | In force since 1 July 2026 | Not subject to §7-306, the state’s net-metering statute, or §7-306.1. Unpaid. |
| Vermont | Act 149 (S.202) | In force since 1 July 2026 | “Shall not be eligible for net metering”; exports “shall not be compensated.” Smart meter required. Unpaid. |
| Maine | LD 1730, ch. 644 | In force since 29 July 2026 | “May not be used for net energy billing.” Unpaid. |
| Colorado | HB26-1007 | In force since 12 August 2026 | Silent: bars utility approval and fees, says nothing about credit. Assume unpaid. |
| Connecticut | Public Act 26-127, sec. 9 | From 1 October 2026 | Device must warn that excess generation is “charged to the customer as usage” unless the customer has a net-metering meter. Unpaid, possibly billed. |
| Virginia | HB 395 / SB 250 | From 1 January 2027 | Excluded from the definition of an eligible customer-generator for net metering. Unpaid. |
| New Hampshire | SB 540, ch. 262 | From 1 January 2027 | Exempt from interconnection review; no provision pays for exports. Assume unpaid. |
| New Jersey | P.L.2026, c.82 | From 1 March 2027 | Exempt from interconnection and metering requirements; silent on payment. Assume unpaid. |
| New York | SUNNY Act, S8512C / A9111C | Passed both chambers; awaits the Governor's signature | Exports “shall be uncompensated” unless the customer voluntarily enters a net-metering or other compensation agreement. Unpaid. |
| California | SB 868 | On the Governor’s desk; he has until 30 September 2026 to act | Silent. Assume unpaid. |

Silence is not a credit: where a law says nothing, balco.nyc assumes no payment unless a utility publishes a tariff for plug-in devices. New York’s bill leaves one door open: an owner may voluntarily enter an interconnection or net-metering agreement, and exports stay unpaid unless they do. Getting paid, in other words, means doing the paperwork the bill otherwise waives. Size limits, certification and the right to install are in the [side-by-side comparison of the laws](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared), and New York in detail on [the SUNNY Act page](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act).

## Does the meter spin backwards?

“Spinning backwards” is the old picture of net metering: while you export, the meter subtracts, and you are billed for the difference. Whether anything like that happens with a plug-in panel depends on the meter, not the law. The Maryland Public Service Commission’s balcony-solar guidance describes what a meter that cannot track exports may do: treat the surplus as zero consumption, or add it to your consumption in error, depending on the meter type. That gives three possibilities.

- **Not counted.** The surplus vanishes from the bill in both directions. This is the outcome balco.nyc’s figures assume: you lose its value and nothing more.

- **Counted as usage.** A meter that registers power flowing either way as consumption bills you at the full retail rate for electricity you gave away. Connecticut’s law requires every device to carry a warning saying exactly this. In the New York example above, the 240 kWh exported would be billed at about $82 a year, cutting a $124 saving to about **$42**.

- **Netted.** A meter set up for net metering does subtract exports. That is the only version of “spinning backwards” that pays you, and under these laws it comes with a net-metering arrangement, not with the plug.

Utilities are beginning to say which applies. Potomac Edison, a FirstEnergy utility in Maryland, states that its standard service meter has no separate register to track energy a customer feeds back to its system. Vermont’s law allows plug-in devices only on smart-metered service. In New York City, Con Edison describes a net meter for customers enrolled in net metering; what an ordinary meter records when power flows out is worth asking Con Edison before the SUNNY Act, which awaits the Governor's signature, takes effect. The practical step is the same everywhere: ask your utility, in writing, how your meter records power flowing out of the apartment.

## How much of the output an apartment actually uses

The share you use depends on how much the panel produces in each hour and how much the apartment draws in that hour. The second has a hard lower limit. Every home has a floor it never drops below: the fridge, the router, standby electronics, smoke alarms. NRDC’s 2015 study of smart-meter data from 70,000 northern California homes found that floor, the lowest hourly level, averaged **218 W**; the one multifamily home in its ten-home audit, occupied by a couple it described as unusually energy-conscious, idled at 92 W. A smaller apartment will usually sit below the study average, so 100 to 300 W brackets most floors.

balco.nyc set the hourly New York output against a constant load at each of those levels. A constant floor is what an apartment draws with nobody home, so these shares hold even for an apartment empty all day; daytime cooking, working or laundry raises them.

| Apartment’s steady draw | 400 W system (302 kWh/yr) | 800 W system (604 kWh/yr) | 1,200 W system (906 kWh/yr) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 W | 72% | 46% | 34% |
| 150 W | 87% | 60% | 46% |
| 200 W | 95% | 72% | 56% |
| 300 W | ~100% | 87% | 72% |

Share of annual output used at home: New York City, vertical south-facing railing, PVWatts V8 hourly, 0.95 railing factor, no shading. For an 800 W railing, most apartments will use between about 60% and 90% of the output; a small, efficient apartment that is empty in the daytime can use less than half. Hourly averages flatter these figures slightly, since passing cloud and a cycling fridge make supply and demand miss each other within the hour; real loads sitting above the floor for much of the day push the other way.

The surplus is seasonal, and not in the direction most people expect. A vertical south-facing panel meets the low winter sun almost head-on, so in New York it produces most in winter: 69 kWh in January against 30 kWh in June, with midday peaks near 690 W. Against a 150 W floor only 43% of January’s output is used at home; in June, 96%. The kilowatt-hours given away are winter ones, which in New York are the cheaper ones, since Con Edison’s delivery charges are higher from June through September (see [what a kWh costs](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate)).

**Why a 400 W system uses more of its output than a 1,200 W one.** The apartment’s load does not grow when you add panels. Every extra panel produces in the same midday hours as the first, when the floor is already covered, so most of its output is surplus. At a 150 W floor, going from 400 to 800 W adds 302 kWh a year of output but only 102 kWh used at home; going from 800 to 1,200 W adds another 302 kWh of output and only **49 kWh** used, about $17 a year at 34¢. The table has a simple symmetry that shows why: a 400 W system against a 150 W floor behaves exactly like an 800 W system against 300 W. What matters is the ratio of system size to what the apartment draws.

## What self-consumption does to payback

Because surplus earns nothing, savings scale directly with the share you use, and payback stretches with it. The table runs the calculator’s own payback loop — a 3% annual rise in the electricity price, 0.5% yearly panel degradation, no discounting — for an unshaded 800 W south-facing railing in each state’s largest city, on the $1,200 mid-range kit, at three self-consumption levels.

| State (city) | Output | Price used | 100% used | 80% used | 60% used |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| New York (NYC) | 604 kWh | 34¢ Con Edison marginal | $205/yr · 5.5 yrs | $164/yr · 6.8 yrs | $123/yr · 8.8 yrs |
| Illinois (Chicago) | 616 kWh | 18.54¢ EIA average | $114/yr · 9.4 yrs | $91/yr · 11.5 yrs | $69/yr · 14.7 yrs |
| California (Los Angeles) | 720 kWh | 32.89¢ EIA average | $237/yr · 4.8 yrs | $190/yr · 6.0 yrs | $142/yr · 7.8 yrs |

First-year saving and nominal payback; output is PVWatts V8 for each city less the 0.95 railing factor. The Illinois and California prices are EIA averages for the 12 months to June 2026, which include fixed monthly charges and so overstate what an avoided kWh is worth. Illinois has no plug-in law (its bill stalled in 2026) and California’s awaits the Governor; they show a cheap-power state and a sunny, expensive one.

At 60% self-consumption, payback is about 1.6 times the 100% figure in all three. In New York, 60% is what the hourly run gives an empty apartment with a 150 W floor, so the 5.5-year headline becomes 8.8. In Illinois it becomes 14.7 years, well over half the 25-year span the calculator models. The self-consumption shares are computed for New York’s sun; Chicago and Los Angeles will differ somewhat at the same floor, but the direction is the same. [Whether balcony solar is worth it](https://balco.nyc/is-balcony-solar-worth-it) sets out the 100% figures for every state.

## Batteries, timers and system size

A battery stores midday surplus for the evening, so its value is capped by how much surplus there is. balco.nyc ran the same hourly New York data with a 2 kWh battery (1.92 kWh usable, 90% round-trip efficiency) that captures each day’s surplus up to its capacity and releases all of it in the evening — a generous setup that ignores the battery’s own standby draw. The last column applies the calculator’s 3% annual price rise.

| Apartment’s steady draw | kWh shifted a year | Worth at 34¢ | Price at which it pays back in 10 years |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 W | 262 | $89 | about $1,020 |
| 150 W | 201 | $68 | about $780 |
| 200 W | 149 | $51 | about $580 |
| 300 W | 72 | $24 | about $280 |

The more you already use, the less a battery has to work with; at balcony scale the ceiling is tens of dollars a year. Modeling in Germany points the same way: the nonprofit balkon.solar, using HTW Berlin’s plug-in solar simulator with a vertical west-facing array and no pay for exports, found a 2 kWh battery stretched payback from 5–6 years to about 13 for small households with small arrays, improving to about 8 only with larger arrays and higher consumption.

The cheaper ways to use more of the output cost nothing. Put the dishwasher, the washing machine or a laptop charger on a timer for the middle of the day, especially from October to March, when a south-facing railing has the most to give. And weigh size by the marginal panel rather than the average one: in the empty-apartment case above, each step up in size buys less than the one before it.

## Common questions

**Do you get paid for balcony solar power you don't use?**

Not under any US plug-in solar law signed as of September 2026. Utah, Maine, Maryland, Vermont and Virginia expressly exclude plug-in devices from net metering, Colorado, New Hampshire and New Jersey say nothing about payment, and Connecticut requires a warning that exports may be billed as usage. New York's SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, says exports are uncompensated unless the owner voluntarily signs a net-metering or other compensation agreement.

**Does my electric meter spin backwards with a plug-in solar panel?**

Only if it is set up for net metering, which plug-in solar laws do not provide by default. On a meter that cannot track exports, the Maryland Public Service Commission says the surplus may be treated as zero consumption or erroneously added to consumption, depending on the meter type. Ask your utility how your meter records power flowing out before plugging a panel in.

**Can a balcony solar panel make my electric bill go up?**

It can on a meter that counts exported power as consumption, which is why Connecticut's plug-in law requires every device to warn that excess generation will be charged as usage unless the customer has a net-metering meter. In balco.nyc's New York example, an 800 W railing in an apartment drawing a steady 150 W exports about 240 kWh a year; billed at Con Edison's 34-cent rate, that would cut a $124 annual saving to about $42.

**How much of a balcony solar system's output does an apartment use?**

It depends on what the apartment draws while the sun is up. balco.nyc's hourly PVWatts model of an 800 W south-facing railing in New York City finds that an apartment drawing a steady 150 W uses about 60% of the output, one drawing 100 W about 46%, and one drawing 300 W about 87%. Those shares assume nobody is home in the daytime; daytime activity raises them.

**Why does a smaller balcony solar system use more of its output?**

Because the apartment's load stays the same while each added panel produces in the same midday hours as the first. In balco.nyc's New York model with a 150 W floor, a 400 W system uses 87% of its output, an 800 W system 60% and a 1,200 W system 46%. The step from 800 to 1,200 W adds about 302 kWh a year of output but only 49 kWh used at home.

**Is a battery worth adding to balcony solar?**

Rarely at balcony scale. In balco.nyc's hourly New York model, a 2 kWh battery on an 800 W railing is worth about $24 to $89 a year at Con Edison's 34-cent rate, depending on how much the apartment already uses, so it would have to cost roughly $280 to $1,020 to pay for itself in 10 years. The more electricity the household already uses in daylight, the less surplus the battery has to store.

## Sources

- [New York State Senate — S8512C (SUNNY Act), text and actions](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S8512/amendment/C): devices “shall not be subject to interconnection or net metering requirements”; exports “shall be uncompensated” unless the customer voluntarily enters a net-metering or other compensation agreement.
- [Connecticut General Assembly — Public Act 26-127, sec. 9](https://www.cga.ct.gov/2026/ACT/PA/PDF/2026PA-00127-R00HB-05340-PA.PDF): the required warning that excess generation is charged to the customer as usage unless the customer has a net-metering meter; effective 1 October 2026.
- [Utah Legislature — H.B. 340 Solar Power Amendments, enrolled copy](https://le.utah.gov/Session/2025/bills/enrolled/HB0340.pdf): portable devices are not subject to net metering program requirements; residential customer generation systems start above 1,200 W.
- [Maine Legislature — LD 1730, Public Law ch. 644 (35-A MRSA §3475)](https://legislature.maine.gov/legis/bills/getPDF.asp?paper=SP0676&item=5&snum=132): eligible plug-in systems “may not be used for net energy billing.”
- [Maryland General Assembly — Chapter 353 of 2026 (HB 1532), PUA §7-321](https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/2026RS/Chapters_noln/CH_353_hb1532e.pdf): portable systems are not subject to §§7-306 (net metering) and 7-306.1, and may not generate renewable energy credits.
- [Vermont Legislature — Act 149 (S.202) as enacted](https://legislature.vermont.gov/Documents/2026/Docs/ACTS/ACT149/ACT149%20As%20Enacted.pdf): plug-in devices only on smart-metered systems, not eligible for net metering, exports not compensated.
- [Virginia Acts of Assembly — Chapter 1052 (HB 395), approved 22 April 2026](https://lis.blob.core.windows.net/files/1225204.PDF): small portable solar generation devices excluded from the definition of an eligible customer-generator for net energy metering.
- [Colorado General Assembly — HB26-1007](https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb26-1007): signed 7 May 2026, effective 12 August 2026; the new §40-2-140 bars utility approval and fees and does not address export credit.
- [Office of the Governor of New Jersey — Garden State Balcony Solar Act signed, 1 September 2026](https://www.nj.gov/governor/news/2026/approved/20260901a.shtml): devices up to 1,200 W exempted from utility interconnection and metering requirements; no export payment described.
- [California Legislative Information — SB 868, enrolled text](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB868): 1,200 W per dwelling; the enrolled text does not address net metering or export compensation.
- [Maryland Public Service Commission — Balcony Solar](https://psc.maryland.gov/regulated-utilities/electricity/renewable-energy/balcony-solar/): a meter that cannot track exports may treat the excess as zero consumption or add it to consumption in error, depending on meter type.
- [FirstEnergy (Potomac Edison) — Maryland interconnection](https://www.firstenergycorp.com/feconnect/maryland.html): Potomac Edison’s standard service meter has no separate register for energy fed back to its system.
- [Con Edison — Solar energy installation FAQ](https://www.coned.com/en/save-money/using-distributed-generation-energy-sources/solar-energy/solar-energy-installation-faq): Con Edison’s description of the net meter used for net-metered solar customers.
- [NREL — PVWatts V8 API documentation](https://developer.nlr.gov/docs/solar/pvwatts/v8/): the hourly AC output (W) behind balco.nyc’s self-consumption and battery computations; the run used the calculator’s parameters and reproduces its 635.7 kWh.
- [NRDC — Home Idle Load: Devices Wasting Huge Amounts of Electricity When Not in Active Use (May 2015)](https://www.nrdc.org/sites/default/files/home-idle-load-IP.pdf): idle load, the lowest hourly smart-meter level, averaged 218 W across 70,000 northern California homes; one audited apartment idled at 92 W.
- [EIA — Form EIA-861M monthly sales and revenue](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia861m/): the data behind balco.nyc’s Illinois (18.54¢) and California (32.89¢) average residential prices: revenue over sales for the 12 months to June 2026.

(January 2026, in German)](https://balkon.solar/news/2026/01/05/fuer-wen-lohnt-sich-ein-steckerspeicher-stand-januar-2026/): HTW Berlin simulator scenarios at €0.33/kWh with no export pay: a 2 kWh battery lengthens payback from 5–6 to about 13 years for small arrays.
