# Can renters install balcony solar?

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-renters  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Usually only with the landlord’s permission. As of 23 September 2026, four states — Vermont, Virginia, New Jersey and Colorado — have signed laws that limit a landlord’s power to refuse, and only Vermont’s protection is in force; the other three start in January or March 2027. balco.nyc’s count of Census data puts 3.3 million renter households, 7.2% of the US total, in those four states, and 76,431 (0.17%) in the one where the protection works today. New York’s SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, and it grants no right to install.

## The short answer, and the four exceptions

A plug-in kit hangs on a railing the landlord owns and plugs into wiring the landlord owns, so in most of the country the lease and the landlord decide. A law that makes plug-in solar *legal* is not one that makes it your *right*: five of the nine signed US plug-in laws stop the utility from demanding approval and give tenants nothing.

balco.nyc read the enacted text of every law in its [state tracker](https://balco.nyc/states). Four limit a landlord’s power to refuse: [Vermont](https://balco.nyc/states/vermont) (in force since 1 July 2026; after 10 days’ notice with no answer, the tenant may proceed), [Virginia](https://balco.nyc/states/virginia) (from 1 January 2027; landlords who own more than four rental units), [New Jersey](https://balco.nyc/states/new-jersey) (from 1 March 2027; tenants who pay their own electric bill) and [Colorado](https://balco.nyc/states/colorado) (from 1 January 2027; no person may “unreasonably prohibit” a device). All four still let the landlord impose reasonable restrictions.

balco.nyc’s count from the Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey puts **3,334,151 renter households** in those four states, 7.2% of the 46.1 million in the United States. Until the 2027 start dates, the protected group is Vermont’s 76,431 renter households: **0.17% of American renters**. New York alone has 3,575,503 renter households, more than the four states combined, and its [SUNNY Act](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act) would give none of them a right to install. Everyone else needs permission.

> **Not legal advice.** This page summarizes statutes and bills as of 23 September 2026. Your lease, your state’s law and any association rules decide your case, and a law that is signed but not yet in effect protects nobody.

## Every tenant provision, compared

balco.nyc’s compilation of every US plug-in solar law or 2026 bill that addresses tenants, from the legislatures’ own pages, as of 23 September 2026. Quoted words are statutory or bill text. The rest of each law (caps, certification, utility notice) is in [the provision-by-provision comparison](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared).

| State | Law or bill | Status | Who it protects, and how | What the landlord keeps |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vermont | Act 149 (S.202) | In force 1 Jul 2026 | All tenants, for a device that meets the Act (UL 3700 or equivalent, 1,200 W per meter). 10 days’ notice; “If the landlord does not respond within 10 days, the tenant may proceed with installation.” | “Any reasonable restrictions,” including making the tenant pay a licensed electrician for any electrical work. No electrical work without the landlord’s permission. |
| Virginia | HB 395 / SB 250 (Chs. 1052, 998) | Signed 22 Apr 2026; effective 1 Jan 2027 | “No landlord who owns more than four rental dwelling units” (or more than a 10% interest in more than four) “shall prohibit a tenant from installing” a device “on the exterior of the tenant’s premises.” 7 days’ notice with documentation. Not units on a ratio utility billing system. | Reasonable restrictions on “size, place, and manner of placement”; may bar devices elsewhere on the premises. The tenant is responsible for any damage. |
| New Jersey | P.L.2026, c.82 (S2368 / A4836) | Signed 1 Sep 2026; effective 1 Mar 2027 | Tenants who pay their own electric bill, within their leased premises including a balcony or patio. 14 days’ written notice with documentation.* | Reasonable restrictions on the device’s physical dimensions, placement and manner of placement; no blanket ban.* |
| Colorado | HB26-1007 (C.R.S. 40-2-140) | In force 12 Aug 2026; tenant clause from 1 Jan 2027 | “A person shall not directly or indirectly unreasonably prohibit” a device. The Act does not mention landlords or tenants. | “Reasonable restrictions,” including prior notice and limits aimed at fire or electrical overload, damage, and the device’s location. |
| Illinois | SB 3104 (House: HB 4524) | Pending; re-referred to Assignments 22 May 2026 | Landlords could not enforce a lease that “unreasonably restricts or prohibits” a system.* | As amended, the bill bars systems over 391 W until the National Electrical Code has a standard for them. |
| North Carolina | HB 1129 | Pending; in House Rules since 30 Apr 2026 | Tenants of landlords who own more than four rental dwellings. 7 days’ notice. | Size and placement limits only “if required to prevent” blocked egress or “unreasonable property damage.” |
| Oregon | HB 4080 | Died in committee, March 2026 | Would have limited restrictions by landlords, HOAs and condo associations.* | — |
| Washington | SSB 6050 | Died in Senate Rules, 2026 | A landlord could not require its approval, or any fee, before a tenant used a device. | — |
| South Carolina | H 4579 | Died in committee, 2026 | A lease or rental agreement “must not prohibit or have the effect of prohibiting” a balcony solar panel. | — |

* New Jersey’s row is summarized from the Governor’s signing announcement, published legal summaries and balco.nyc’s state tracker; the Illinois and Oregon rows are from the legislatures’ official bill digests, not the bill text.

**Laws with nothing for tenants.** [Utah](https://balco.nyc/states/utah), [Maryland](https://balco.nyc/states/maryland), [Connecticut](https://balco.nyc/states/connecticut), [New Hampshire](https://balco.nyc/states/new-hampshire) and [Maine](https://balco.nyc/states/maine) have signed plug-in laws with no tenant right; Maine’s only requires anyone installing on a structure they do not own to protect it and restore it on removal, a duty rather than a right. The same silence runs through [New York](https://balco.nyc/states/new-york)’s SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature; [California](https://balco.nyc/states/california)’s SB 868, awaiting the Governor’s decision; and pending bills in [Massachusetts](https://balco.nyc/states/massachusetts), [Michigan](https://balco.nyc/states/michigan), [Pennsylvania](https://balco.nyc/states/pennsylvania) and the [District of Columbia](https://balco.nyc/states/district-of-columbia). Tracker summaries saying the Massachusetts and Pennsylvania bills protect tenants describe provisions balco.nyc could not find in either text.

## How many renters the laws reach

A law’s reach is a head count, so balco.nyc made one: renter-occupied homes (households) by state from the Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey 1-year estimates, table **B25003** (Tenure). That is the newest 1-year release; on 4 August 2026 the Bureau said the 2025 release date “is being determined.” Two laws cover only some tenants, so each gets a narrower estimate:

- **Virginia** turns on how many units the landlord owns, which no Census table records. The nearest proxy is renters in buildings of five or more units (table **B25032**): 555,373, or 49.0% of the state’s renters.

- **New Jersey** turns on paying your own electric bill. The published tables do not split electricity billing by tenure, but **B25069** records renters who pay extra for at least one utility: 1,152,187, against 126,937 who pay for none. The first figure is a ceiling.

| State | Renter households (B25003) | Narrower estimate | What the narrower figure counts | Protection starts |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vermont | 76,431 | 76,431 | All tenants | 1 Jul 2026 |
| Colorado | 844,547 | 844,547 | All tenants | 1 Jan 2027 |
| Virginia | 1,134,049 | 555,373 | Renters in buildings of 5+ units (B25032) | 1 Jan 2027 |
| New Jersey | 1,279,124 | 1,152,187 | Renters paying for at least one utility (B25069) | 1 Mar 2027 |
| Four states | 3,334,151 | 2,628,538 |  |  |
| Share of US renter households (46,101,640) | 7.2% | 5.7% |  |  |

The arithmetic: 76,431 + 844,547 + 1,134,049 + 1,279,124 = 3,334,151, and 3,334,151 ÷ 46,101,640 = 7.2%; the narrower column sums to 2,628,538, or 5.7%. The Census margin of error on the four-state total is about ±25,000 at 90% confidence. For scale, New York has 3,575,503 renter households (45.7% of its households), and the five states with a plug-in law but no tenant clause hold 1,939,324 renter households for whom plugging in is, or will shortly be, legal and the landlord still decides.

The same data qualifies a figure in New Jersey’s signing announcement, where an advocate says the law benefits “roughly 40 percent of New Jerseyans who rent or live in apartments.” That counts people and includes apartment owners, who fall under the law’s association provisions, not its tenant clause. By households, the ACS puts renters at 36.1% of the state’s total (1,279,124 of 3,543,944), and the tenant clause reaches at most 32.5% (1,152,187).

What these numbers are not: they count households, not balconies. The ACS does not ask whether a home has a balcony, a patio or an outdoor outlet, so the renters who could actually use these protections are fewer than every figure above, by an amount nobody has measured. The Virginia proxy is loose both ways: it includes condo units rented out by small owners, who are not covered, and units on ratio utility billing, which the law excludes; it misses houses owned by large landlords, who are covered.

## What “can’t prohibit” still allows

None of the four laws hands the balcony to the tenant. Read closely, they replace a landlord’s veto with a landlord’s conditions:

- **Reasonable restrictions survive everywhere.** Virginia names “size, place, and manner of placement” and lets the landlord bar devices anywhere but the exterior of the tenant’s premises; Colorado lists notice, fire and overload risk, damage and location. What is reasonable has not been tested in any of the four states.

- **Notice comes first.** Seven days in Virginia, with documentation that the device qualifies and where it will go; ten in Vermont; fourteen, in writing, in New Jersey. The laws protect a tenant who gives notice before installing.

- **Wiring stays the landlord’s.** Vermont says a landlord “shall not be compelled to perform or pay for electrical work”; Virginia requires express written approval for anything that alters wiring or panels. If your balcony has no outdoor outlet, none of these laws gets you one.

- **Damage is the tenant’s.** Virginia makes the tenant responsible for any damage the device causes.

- **Only a qualifying device is protected.** Vermont covers devices certified to UL 3700 “or an equivalent certification.” No complete plug-in system is certified to UL 3700 as of September 2026 (components are), so a Vermont tenant’s protection depends on whether a kit’s listing counts as equivalent, which the Act does not settle. New Jersey also accepts a comparable standard; Virginia and Colorado ask for certification or listing by a nationally recognized testing laboratory.

- **Surplus power earns nothing.** Vermont says exports “shall not be compensated,” Virginia excludes the devices from net metering, and New Jersey and Colorado are silent. Assume what you do not use is given away.

- **Association rules may still bind.** Virginia’s law does not override condominium or HOA documents, so a tenant in a rented condo can be protected against the landlord and still refused by the association; New Jersey’s and Colorado’s bind associations too. See [condos, co-ops and HOAs](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-condo-hoa).

## Asking your landlord: a checklist and a letter

In most states the request is the whole process; in the four above it doubles as the statutory notice. A specific written request is easier to approve than a general one. Do the physical checks first with [the installation guide](https://balco.nyc/install-balcony-solar); if the landlord’s worry is fire or shock, [the safety evidence](https://balco.nyc/is-plug-in-solar-safe) is summarized separately. Include:

- **The device:** make, model, panel count, maximum AC output, and the certification exactly as the listing states it, including the anti-islanding feature each of the four laws requires.

- **Size and weight** of the panels with brackets.

- **Mounting without drilling:** clamps or hooks inside the railing, nothing fixed to the facade, secured against wind.

- **The outlet:** which existing outdoor outlet, whether it is GFCI-protected and covered, no extension cord, and no new wiring without written approval.

- **Insurance:** your renters policy’s liability limit, and acceptance of responsibility for damage.

- **Removal** at move-out, or on short notice for building work, with the railing restored.

- **The law, if one applies:** the statute and the notice period.

> **A neutral template.** Dear [landlord or managing agent], I would like to install a small plug-in solar system on the balcony of [unit]. The details are below, and I am happy to discuss any conditions. *Device:* [make and model], [number] panels, [watts] maximum AC output, listed to [standard] by [laboratory]. It switches off automatically if grid power is lost. Specification sheet attached. *Size and mounting:* [dimensions], [total weight]. It clamps to the inside of the railing; nothing is drilled into or fixed to the building. *Power:* it plugs into the existing outdoor outlet at [location]. No extension cord and no change to the wiring. *Insurance:* my renters policy with [insurer] carries [amount] of liability coverage, and I will be responsible for any damage the system causes. *Removal:* I will remove it and restore the railing when I move out, or within [number] days if you need access for building work. [If a state law applies: I am giving this notice under [statute], [number] days before installation on [date].] I would be grateful for your written approval, or for any conditions you would attach.

The template is a starting point, not legal advice. Where a statute applies, match its wording: Virginia’s notice, for example, must include documentation that the device meets the law’s definition and identify the proposed location.

## If the answer is no

Outside the four states, a refusal usually stands until the lease changes. A no to a vague request is sometimes a yes to a specific one: a smaller system, a floor stand instead of a railing mount, proof of insurance, a firm removal commitment. Lease renewal is a natural moment to ask again.

Where one of the four laws covers you, the landlord can restrict but not refuse, and a dispute over what is “reasonable” goes through the ordinary landlord-tenant channels. In [New York](https://balco.nyc/states/new-york) the SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, and nothing in it limits a landlord’s answer: [renters will need permission after it is signed, as they do now](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act).

Before asking at all, check it is worth asking. Output depends mostly on how much sky the balcony sees, which is [a kilowatt-hour number, not a yes or no](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight); the [calculator](https://balco.nyc/) gives it for any US address, and a shaded balcony may not pay back in the time you expect to stay.

## Common questions

**Can my landlord stop me from installing balcony solar?**

In most US states, yes: a plug-in kit attaches to a railing and outlet the landlord owns, so the lease and the landlord decide. As of September 2026 four states have signed laws limiting that power. Vermont's protection is in force; Virginia's and Colorado's start on 1 January 2027 and New Jersey's on 1 March 2027. Even there, the landlord may impose reasonable restrictions.

**Which states give renters a right to install plug-in solar?**

Vermont (in force since 1 July 2026, 10 days' notice), Virginia (from 1 January 2027, tenants of landlords owning more than four rental units, excluding ratio-utility-billed units), New Jersey (from 1 March 2027, tenants who pay their own electric bill, 14 days' written notice) and Colorado (from 1 January 2027, no unreasonable prohibition). Tenant bills in Illinois and North Carolina are pending but stalled.

**Does New York's SUNNY Act let renters install balcony solar?**

No. The SUNNY Act (S8512C / A9111C) has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, and it contains no landlord or tenant provision. A New York renter would still need the landlord's permission after it is signed.

**How many renters do state balcony solar tenant protections cover?**

balco.nyc's count from the Census Bureau's 2024 American Community Survey (table B25003) puts 3,334,151 renter households, 7.2% of the US total, in Vermont, Virginia, New Jersey and Colorado; about 2.6 million (5.7%) narrowed to the tenants each law covers. Until 2027 only Vermont's 76,431, or 0.17%, are protected.

**Does my landlord have to add an outdoor outlet for balcony solar?**

No. None of the four state laws with tenant provisions requires a landlord to add wiring. Vermont's says a landlord shall not be compelled to perform or pay for electrical work, and Virginia's requires the landlord's express written approval for anything that alters wiring or electrical panels.

**What should a balcony solar request to a landlord include?**

The device's make, model, AC wattage and certification; its size and weight; how it mounts without drilling; which existing outdoor outlet it uses, with no extension cord; your renters insurance and acceptance of responsibility for damage; removal and restoration at move-out; and, where a state tenant law applies, the statute and notice period.

# Is there a tax credit for balcony solar in 2026?

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-tax-credit  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

No. The 30% federal Residential Clean Energy Credit (IRC §25D) does not cover anything installed in 2026: the One Big Beautiful Bill Act ended it for expenditures made after 31 December 2025, and the IRS counts an expenditure as made when installation is completed, not when you pay. On a $1,200 mid-range kit the credit would have been worth $360. balco.nyc’s PVWatts runs for the largest city in every state put the median payback at 9.9 years at full price against 7.1 years at $840, so losing the credit adds a median 2.7 years.

## No federal credit in 2026, and what it would have been worth

The credit solar sellers used to quote was the Residential Clean Energy Credit in section 25D of the Internal Revenue Code: 30% of the cost of qualified solar electric property, with no dollar cap. Section 70506 of Public Law 119-21, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed on 4 July 2025, rewrote its termination clause so that the credit “shall not apply with respect to any expenditures made after December 31, 2025.” The same act ended the separate home-improvement credit in section 25C. There is no replacement federal credit for a household buying solar in 2026, plug-in or rooftop.

To put a number on what went away, balco.nyc reran its state-by-state payback with the credit restored. The method is the one behind the [state pages](https://balco.nyc/states): an 800 W kit on an unshaded south-facing railing in each state’s largest city, NREL PVWatts V8 output multiplied by the 0.95 railing factor for a vertical panel, valued at the state’s EIA average residential price for the 12 months to June 2026, with output falling 0.5% a year and prices rising 3% a year. The only thing that changes is the price: $1,200 for a mid-range kit, or $840 after a 30% credit.

| State (reference city) | Output, kWh/yr | Average price | Payback at $1,200 | Payback at $840 | Credit was worth |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Maine (Portland) | 692 | 28.99¢ | 5.6 years | 4.0 years | 1.6 years |
| New York (New York City) | 604 | 27.96¢ | 6.6 years | 4.7 years | 1.9 years |
| Maryland (Baltimore) | 673 | 20.75¢ | 7.9 years | 5.7 years | 2.2 years |
| Colorado (Denver) | 805 | 16.45¢ | 8.3 years | 6.0 years | 2.3 years |
| Utah (Salt Lake City) | 724 | 13.36¢ | 10.9 years | 8.0 years | 3.0 years |
| Median, 50 states and DC | — | — | 9.9 years | 7.1 years | 2.7 years |

Three things follow from the full 51-row run. The credit was worth most, in years, where electricity is cheapest: 1.6 years in Maine, 3.0 in Utah, and 3.7 in Washington, which has the longest payback of the 51. With the credit, the mid-range kit would pay back inside ten years in 50 of the 51; at full price, 28 do. And a 30% price cut shortens payback by a little less than 30% — a median 28% — because the years it removes are the late ones, when rising prices make each year’s saving larger. Differences in the table are computed before rounding.

Every figure here is a ceiling, not an expectation. It assumes an unshaded railing and that every kilowatt-hour is used in the home, since the model treats surplus power as earning nothing, which is how most of the new plug-in laws work. The EIA figures are averages that include fixed monthly charges a panel does not reduce, which flatters the value of each kWh. New York’s row uses the state average, not the 34¢ Con Edison marginal rate balco.nyc uses for [New York City addresses](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate).

## When an expenditure counted as “made”

The cut-off is not the day you paid. Section 25D(e)(8)(A) has long said that an expenditure is treated as made “when the original installation of the item is completed.” In its August 2025 questions and answers on the new law (Fact Sheet 2025-05, question 7), the IRS applied that rule to the termination directly: paying on or before 31 December 2025 does not preserve the credit if installation is completed afterwards.

For a plug-in kit the consequence is plain. A kit bought in December 2025 but mounted and switched on in January 2026 is outside the credit on the IRS’s reading. The IRS has not said what “installation completed” means for a device you clamp to a railing and plug in yourself. The natural reading is the day it was mounted and running, but we could not find the point addressed anywhere.

The IRS’s own credit page words the cut-off differently — the credit “is not available for any property placed in service after December 31, 2025” — and tells filers to claim it for the year the property “is installed, not merely purchased.” Both formulations point the same way, and the statute’s test, the one the IRS applied in its FAQ, is completed installation.

What survives is narrow. A system installed in 2025 is claimed on the 2025 return, and the IRS says a taxpayer who missed it can generally amend within three years of filing or two years of paying the tax, whichever is later. Unused credit carries forward to later years. All of that assumes a plug-in kit was eligible in the first place, which is the question in section 4. None of this is tax advice; a preparer can tell you how it applies to your return.

## Why “30% off with the federal tax credit” is now wrong

Kit listings, comparison pages and articles written before the summer of 2025 often advertise a plug-in kit as “30% off with the federal tax credit,” or print a net price with the credit already subtracted. Many are still online and still turn up in search. For any kit installed in 2026 the claim is wrong for the simplest reason: the credit no longer exists for new installations. Web pages are rarely rewritten when a tax law changes, and a price with 30% taken off is the most flattering number a seller can show.

The claim was loose even while the credit existed. Section 25D was never a discount at checkout. It was a nonrefundable credit claimed on IRS Form 5695 when you filed, limited to the tax you owed that year, with any excess carried forward. A household with little federal income tax got little or nothing in the year it installed the kit. And no seller could promise eligibility: that was between the taxpayer and the IRS, and for plug-in kits the IRS never addressed it.

The practical rule for 2026: compare kits on the sticker price. If a page shows a price “after tax credit,” divide it by 0.7 to recover the real one — an $840 net price is a $1,200 kit. balco.nyc’s own [cost and payback figures](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost) are gross, with no federal credit netted out.

## Did 25D ever clearly cover a plug-in kit?

Plausibly, but nobody with authority said so. The statutory definition is broad: a qualified solar electric property expenditure is one “for property which uses solar energy to generate electricity for use in a dwelling unit” in the United States that the taxpayer uses as a residence (§25D(d)(2)). Nothing in it sets a minimum size or requires a roof, a licensed installer, net metering or the utility’s approval. The IRS’s FAQ adds that the taxpayer may rent the home, which is unusual for a tax break on equipment and mattered for apartment dwellers. For solar, the home did not have to be a main residence either; a second home the taxpayer lived in part-time counted.

What was never settled is how a device built to be moved fits a credit organized around installation. The timing rule keys to “original installation,” the IRS told filers to claim the year the property was installed, and several of the new state laws define plug-in devices as moveable or portable. We found no IRS ruling, FAQ, form instruction or publication that addresses plug-in or portable solar. One edge is clear: a battery bundled with a kit counted as battery storage technology only if its capacity was at least 3 kWh.

There was also a practical wrinkle. On balco.nyc’s state research, Utah was the only state with a plug-in solar law in force during 2025; everywhere else, connecting a kit meant going through the utility’s interconnection rules. The tax code did not make the credit depend on that, but a claim could have rested on an installation the utility had not approved. The honest summary is eligible on the text, untested in practice, and moot for anything installed from 2026.

## State tax breaks in the plug-in states

We checked every state with a plug-in solar law in force or signed — Utah, Maine, Colorado, Maryland, Vermont, Connecticut, Virginia, New Hampshire and New Jersey — plus New York, whose SUNNY Act has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature. None has a state income-tax credit or rebate that plainly covers a self-installed plug-in kit. Five exempt solar equipment from sales tax in wording a kit plausibly fits, though none of the guidance we found mentions plug-in systems.

| State | What exists | Does it fit a plug-in kit? |
|---|---|---|
| New York | Solar energy system equipment credit, 25% up to $5,000 (Tax Law §606(g-1)). State sales-tax exemption for residential solar equipment; New York City charges no local tax on it. | Credit: probably not. The IT-255 instructions require a net-metering contract (or compliance with the utility’s net-metering schedule) and a connection to the utility’s system; the SUNNY Act would exempt plug-in devices from net metering. Sales tax: plausibly, if a kit counts as equipment “installed in a residence”. Claimed with Form ST-121. |
| New Jersey | Sales-tax exemption for solar energy devices that provide electrical power (N.J.S.A. 54:32B-8.33) | Plausibly. Claimed with Form ST-4. |
| Connecticut | Sales-tax exemption for solar electricity generating systems, defined as systems that convert sunlight directly into electricity, including modules, inverters and mounting hardware | Plausibly. Claimed with Form CERT-140. |
| Maryland | Sales-tax exemption for solar energy equipment that generates electricity “to be used in a structure or supplied to the electric grid” (Tax-General §11-230). Maryland Solar Access Program rebate of $750 per kW DC. | Exemption: plausibly. Rebate: no. It is for income-qualified homeowners, requires a participating contractor and pays after interconnection. |
| Colorado | Sales-tax exemption for components that produce alternating-current electricity from a renewable source, including solar modules and inverters | Plausibly, but only for state and some special-district taxes. Most city and county taxes still apply unless adopted locally, and home-rule cities set their own. |
| Vermont | Renewable-energy equipment is generally taxable; the home exemptions cover off-grid systems and solar water heating | No. A plug-in device is grid-connected and cannot be net metered. |
| Utah | Renewable Energy Systems Tax Credit | No. Residential solar installed in 2024 or later is not eligible. |
| New Hampshire | Residential Renewable Electrical Generation Rebate | No. The program is permanently closed. |
| Maine, Virginia | We found no state credit, rebate or sales-tax exemption that applies | We could not confirm that none exists. |

An exemption is worth the sales tax you would otherwise pay. New York City is the largest case: residential solar equipment is exempt from the 4% state tax and the 0.375% Metropolitan Commuter Transportation District tax, and the city’s own rate on it is zero, so a qualifying $1,200 kit would avoid the full 8.875% combined rate, or **$106.50**. That is under a third of the $360 the federal credit used to be worth, and it depends on a retailer accepting an exemption certificate for a product the rules never contemplated. Ask before you pay: the exemption is normally claimed by giving the seller a certificate at the time of sale. In New York the question is also premature, since until the SUNNY Act is signed and takes effect the utility’s approval is still required to connect a kit.

This is not legal or tax advice. Sales-tax treatment can turn on facts the published guidance does not address, local rates vary, and we found no state agency that has ruled on a plug-in kit. For what each state’s law allows, see [how the state laws compare](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-laws-compared) or the individual [state pages](https://balco.nyc/states); for whether a kit is worth buying at full price, see [is balcony solar worth it](https://balco.nyc/is-balcony-solar-worth-it).

## Common questions

**Is there a federal tax credit for balcony solar in 2026?**

No. The 30% Residential Clean Energy Credit under section 25D of the Internal Revenue Code was ended by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Public Law 119-21, signed 4 July 2025) for expenditures made after 31 December 2025. There is no replacement federal credit for household solar, plug-in or rooftop.

**I paid for a balcony solar kit in December 2025 but set it up in January 2026. Can I claim the 30% credit?**

Not on the IRS's reading. Section 25D treats an expenditure as made when the original installation is completed, and the IRS's August 2025 FAQ says that paying on or before 31 December 2025 does not preserve the credit if installation was completed afterwards.

**Did the 30% federal credit ever cover plug-in balcony solar?**

Plausibly, but it was never confirmed. The statute covers property that uses solar energy to generate electricity for use in a home the taxpayer lives in, including a rented one, with no minimum size or interconnection requirement. But the credit is organized around installation, and the IRS never issued guidance on plug-in or portable systems. The question is moot for anything installed from 2026.

**How much longer does balcony solar take to pay back without the tax credit?**

balco.nyc's model of an 800 W kit on a south-facing railing in each state's largest city puts the median payback on a $1,200 kit at 9.9 years, against 7.1 years at the $840 it would have cost after a 30% credit: about 2.7 years longer. The gap ranges from 1.4 years in California to 3.7 years in Washington, and every figure is a ceiling that assumes no shade and full self-consumption.

**Does New York's solar tax credit apply to a plug-in balcony system?**

Probably not. New York's solar energy system equipment credit (25% up to $5,000) requires, for systems that make electricity, a net-metering contract with the utility or compliance with its net-metering schedule, and a connection to the utility's system. The SUNNY Act, which has passed both chambers and awaits the Governor's signature, would exempt plug-in devices from net metering. We could not confirm how the two would interact.

**Is a balcony solar kit exempt from sales tax?**

In some states, plausibly. New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Maryland and Colorado exempt solar equipment from sales tax in wording a plug-in kit appears to fit, though no guidance we found mentions plug-in systems, and Colorado's exemption covers only state and some special-district taxes. Vermont's does not fit a grid-connected plug-in device. The exemption is normally claimed with a certificate at the time of sale.

**Are there state rebates for balcony solar?**

None that we found for a self-installed plug-in kit in the states with plug-in laws. Maryland's Solar Access Program requires a participating contractor and interconnection, New Hampshire's residential solar rebate is permanently closed, and Utah's residential solar credit ended for systems installed in 2024 or later.

---

# Does my balcony get enough sun for solar?

URL: https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-04

There is no threshold: the honest answer is a kilowatt-hour number, not a yes or no. In a dense city what sets it is mostly how much sky your balcony can see past the building opposite, and how high up you are — which way it faces matters less than the rules of thumb suggest. A typical 800 W New York system produces 400 to 900 kWh a year, and a high-floor south balcony makes roughly three times what a low-floor north one does.

## “Enough sun” is a number, not a threshold

The standard answer to this question is a rule of thumb: three to four hours of direct sunlight a day and you are fine. It is a reasonable rule and it comes from somewhere sensible — it is roughly the line between a balcony that will grow herbs and one that will not. But it treats the question as a gate you either pass or fail, and that is not how a solar system behaves. A panel does not switch on at four hours. It produces a continuously varying amount all year, and the useful output of that arithmetic is a single figure: annual kilowatt-hours.

That figure is what everything downstream depends on. In New York the number to multiply it by is Con Edison’s all-in marginal rate of about **$0.34 per kilowatt-hour** — supply, delivery and surcharges together, which is [the correct rate for electricity you generate and consume yourself](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate). A typical 800 W system on an NYC balcony lands somewhere between **400 and 900 kWh a year**, so the annual saving runs from roughly $136 to roughly $306. On a $1,200 mid-range kit that is the difference between a [payback of under four years and one of over eight](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost). Both of those balconies get “enough” sun in the sense that the panels work. Only one of them is a good idea.

This is also where a widely repeated figure needs qualifying. You will often read that an 800 W kit covers 15–25% of an apartment’s electricity. That is a nameplate-ideal number with no shading derate applied. Against the EIA’s New York average household consumption of about 6,850 kWh a year, the real 400–900 kWh band works out at **6% to 13%** — and the lower end of that is not a rounding error, it is what a shaded low-floor balcony actually delivers. The 15–25% figure describes a well-sited system belonging to a light consumer. It is a ceiling, not an expectation.

> **One number, not a verdict.** If someone answers “does my balcony get enough sun” with yes or no, they have skipped the only part of the answer that changes what you should do.

## The four things that decide it, in order

Most solar guidance is written for a detached house, where orientation is the first question because it is very nearly the only one. In a dense city the ranking inverts. Here is the order that actually matters for an NYC balcony:

|  | Variable | What it really is | Why it ranks here |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Obstruction | The height of the building across the street relative to yours, and how far away it stands | It sets the floor of the sky you can see. On a low floor in a narrow canyon it can remove the entire middle of the day for months at a time — a bigger swing than every other variable combined. You cannot change it, and it is the one nobody asks about. |
| 2 | Floor height | How far above the street the panel sits | Every storey you climb drops the skyline. The same balcony, facing the same way, is a materially different proposition on the 3rd floor and the 12th. Published research on vertical facade PV finds incident energy distributed non-uniformly along the height of the wall for exactly this reason. |
| 3 | Orientation | The compass direction the railing faces | Real, predictable and correctly priced by any decent model — but it only prices sun you can actually see. Orientation decides how you use an open sky; obstruction decides whether you have one. |
| 4 | Tilt | Flat against the railing (vertical, 90°) or angled out on a bracket | The only variable you get to choose, and the one most often taken away by the railing design or the building’s rules. balco.nyc models four mount angles — 35°, 60°, 70° and vertical — because the gap between them is worth knowing before you argue with a board. |

This ordering is why one particular claim deserves care. You will find it stated as a constant, across many pages, that a north-facing balcony produces **75% less** than a south-facing one. We could not trace that figure to a primary source; it appears without attribution and gets copied forward. The deeper problem is not the number, it is the framing. It presents azimuth as if it were the whole answer, on a page written for someone whose real constraint is the twelve-storey building forty feet away.

In a city the two effects compete, and obstruction usually wins. **An unobstructed high-floor north balcony can out-produce a south-facing balcony boxed in by a taller building across a narrow street.** balco.nyc’s own modelling puts roughly **3×** between the best and worst realistic NYC cases — a high-floor south balcony against a low-floor north one — and that spread is the *combination* of all four variables, not orientation working alone. Attribute the whole gap to which way you face and you will mis-rank two apartments in the same building.

One local wrinkle before you take the listing at its word: most of Manhattan’s grid is rotated about **29° east of true north**, aligned to the axis of the island rather than to the compass. What a broker calls a north-facing apartment is usually facing north-north-east. That rotation is large enough to change the answer, which is why the calculator asks for an address rather than a direction.

## A street canyon is not a suburban lot

The geometry is worth making concrete, because once you see it the rest of the page follows. A panel receives direct sunlight when the sun is above the skyline in that direction. In the suburbs the skyline is a fence and a maple tree, so it sits a few degrees above the horizon and the sun clears it for most of the day. The sun’s path is the story. In a street canyon the skyline is a wall, it can sit thirty or forty degrees up, and the sun’s path is just the thing that does or does not cross it.

Take a standard Manhattan side street. The Commissioners’ Plan of 1811 set cross streets at **60 feet** (about 18 m) building face to building face, and avenues at 100 feet. Put a six-storey building — roughly 18 m — directly opposite, and ask how high the sun has to climb before it reaches your railing:

| Your floor | Panel height above street | Sun must be above | Clears the 21 Dec noon sun (26°)? | Clears the equinox noon sun (49°)? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2nd | 4 m | 37° | No | Yes |
| 4th | 10 m | 24° | Barely | Yes |
| 6th | 16 m | 6° | Yes | Yes |
| 8th and up | 22 m+ | Clear | Yes | Yes |

Nothing about that table depends on which way the balcony faces. A second-floor apartment on that street has no direct midday sun for weeks around the winter solstice whether it is south-facing or not, because the sun never gets high enough to clear the parapet opposite. Six floors up, on the same facade, the obstruction has essentially vanished. That is the whole argument for putting address and height ahead of azimuth.

Two things make the real city messier than the table, both in the same direction. Buildings are rarely a uniform wall — a setback, a gap at the corner, a lower neighbour mid-block can open a wedge of sky that changes a balcony’s year. And the obstruction that matters is not only the one across the street: the wing of your own building, the tower on the diagonal, and the balcony slab immediately above you all take a bite. This is why a real answer needs a model of the actual surrounding block rather than a street width and a rule.

## Diffuse light, and why a north balcony is not zero

Sunlight arrives in two forms. **Beam** (or direct) radiation travels in a straight line from the disc of the sun, and it is what casts a shadow. **Diffuse** radiation has been scattered by the atmosphere and by cloud, and it arrives from the whole dome of the sky at once. Panels convert both. Almost every intuition people have about balconies concerns only the first.

The split matters more than the vocabulary suggests. In the northeastern United States roughly **40% of annual global horizontal irradiance is diffuse**, which is the figure balco.nyc’s shadow model uses for its beam/diffuse constants (see [the methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology)). On a clear day the diffuse share is small; on an overcast day it is essentially everything, and under a fully overcast sky *surface orientation stops being a significant variable at all*. Roughly two-fifths of the year’s energy, then, does not care which way your railing points. It cares how much sky your railing can see.

That is the honest case for a north-facing balcony, and it is a real one. A vertical panel sees half the sky dome no matter which direction it faces. Diffuse light is not free of the city — the building opposite blocks its share of that half-dome exactly as it blocks the beam — but what it takes away is set by obstruction, not by compass direction. A north balcony’s output is not a fraction of a south balcony’s because of some efficiency penalty; it is lower because it has given up most of its beam.

Most, but not all. The sun rises north of due east between the equinoxes: at the June solstice in New York it comes up at an azimuth of about **58°** and sets at about **302°**. A true-north-facing wall therefore has the sun in front of it for around seven hours of a fifteen-hour midsummer day. The catch is that all of those hours are at a glancing angle with the sun low in the sky, so the beam they deliver is modest. And from the September equinox to the March equinox, a true-north vertical panel receives **essentially no direct sunlight at all** — the sun rises and sets south of the east–west line for the entire winter half of the year. Everything it produces in those six months is diffuse.

Here the Manhattan grid rotation earns its keep again. A balcony facing 29° rather than 0° meets the summer morning sun much closer to head-on, and still catches a couple of hours of direct sun around the equinoxes, when a true-north wall catches none. A “north-facing” NYC apartment and a true-north-facing one are not the same object.

## Winter, honestly

Winter is where the two halves of this page collide, and where the standard reassurance is most misleading. The reassurance goes: photovoltaic cells are *more* efficient when cold, so winter is not the problem you think. The first clause is true. Cell efficiency does improve below the 25°C rating temperature, which is why the same panel makes slightly more per unit of sunlight in February than in July. The second clause does not follow from it, and the gap between them is most of the winter story.

What actually costs you output in a New York winter is three things, none of them temperature:

- **Short days.** About **9 hours 15 minutes** of daylight on 21 December, against 15 hours 6 minutes at the June solstice. Roughly 40% fewer hours to work with, before anything else happens.

- **Low sun.** At 40.7°N the sun reaches only about **26°** above the horizon at solar noon on the winter solstice (25.9°, from latitude and the 23.44° solar declination). At the June solstice it reaches 73°.

- **Inter-building shading.** Long shadows down the canyon, all day, at the exact time of year they are hardest to escape.

That third point is the one that gets left out, and it is not an independent penalty — it is caused by the second. Low sun elevation is precisely the condition under which street-canyon shading is worst, because the sun spends the whole day below the parapet opposite instead of above it. Look back at the table in section 3: the second-floor balcony needs the sun above 37° and December offers 26°. A cell-efficiency bonus of a few percent does not touch a balcony that is in shadow from breakfast to dusk.

There is a genuine and rarely mentioned consolation, though, and it applies specifically to balcony systems. A *vertical* panel likes a low sun. A south-facing vertical panel meets the December noon sun almost square on — within about 26° of perpendicular — while in June that same panel watches the noon sun pass 73° overhead and catches very little of it. In pure incidence-angle terms, winter is the season a railing-mounted panel is built for. The reason December is still the worst month in New York is not the panel’s geometry. It is the building across the street.

None of which means winter output is zero. It means winter is the trough, that the depth of the trough is set by your skyline rather than by the thermometer, and that a model which does not simulate your specific block cannot tell you how deep it is.

## Getting the number for your actual address

The usual advice at this point is to go and look: stand on the balcony, note when the sun arrives and leaves, and repeat across the seasons. It is honest advice and it is not wrong — but it asks for a year of your attention to produce an observation, and an observation is still not a kilowatt-hour figure. The winter answer, which is the one that decides whether your worst months are workable, cannot be had before December. A shadow model answers the same question in seconds, because the geometry is entirely known in advance.

That is what balco.nyc does. For any NYC address it assembles three things:

- **The buildings.** NYC PLUTO records and building-footprint data give the heights and shapes of every neighbouring structure **within 200 m**, which are assembled into a 3D scene around your balcony.

- **The sun.** Sun positions are traced against that scene through the year to produce monthly shade factors — how much of the light your balcony would otherwise receive is actually blocked, beam and diffuse separately.

- **The weather.** NREL’s **PVWatts V8** runs an **8,760-hour** simulation over a typical meteorological year for your location, with the panel’s real tilt and azimuth, which is where orientation gets priced properly rather than by rule of thumb.

Stated accuracy is **±15%** on annual production, or ±20% when the client-side fallback is used. That is a *modelled* band and we are explicit about the distinction: it comes from the uncertainty in the inputs and the method, not from comparing predictions against meters. **No metered NYC balcony installation has been compared against this model**, for the straightforward reason that plug-in solar is not yet legal here and so there are very few of them to compare against. The full derivation is on [the methodology page](https://balco.nyc/methodology).

> **Worth knowing before you shop.** Plug-in solar is not yet legal in New York. The SUNNY Act passed both chambers of the Legislature and is awaiting the Governor’s signature; it has not been signed. [What the Act does and does not change](https://balco.nyc/sunny-act) — including that it grants no right to install, so renters and co-op residents still need permission.

## What the model cannot see

A shadow model built from building footprints resolves buildings. Everything smaller than a building is invisible to it, and on a balcony some of those things are two metres from the panel. The honest list:

- **Micro-shading.** A window air-conditioner projecting from the unit above. A street tree at the corner in full leaf from May to October. Your own parapet, or the underside of the balcony slab overhead, which on a deep-set balcony can shade a vertical panel for much of the day. A satellite dish, a laundry rack, a neighbour’s planter. None of these appear in PLUTO.

- **Exactly where the panel goes.** The model assumes the balcony’s facade direction. If you mount at an angle to the railing, hang the panel on the return wall, or shift it to the shadier end to keep the view, your result moves off the modelled figure.

- **Facade detail.** Setbacks, bay windows, cornices and the geometry of your own building’s wings are represented at footprint resolution, which is coarser than the things immediately around a single balcony.

- **Validation against reality.** Stated again because it belongs in this list: the ±15% is modelled, not measured.

This is where a few minutes of your own observation genuinely helps, and it is a different task from watching your balcony for a year. The model has already handled the part that takes a year — the sun’s path, the seasons, the surrounding block. What it needs from you is the part it cannot see: stand at the railing on one clear morning and look for anything within a few metres that casts a shadow onto the spot where the panel would sit. If there is nothing, take the modelled number as it stands. If there is something, treat it as a haircut on that number rather than as a reason to start over.

Then run the address. If you have not read [what a plug-in system actually is](https://balco.nyc/what-is-balcony-solar) or [what one costs in New York](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost), those are the two pages that turn a kilowatt-hour figure into a decision.

## Common questions

**How many hours of direct sun does a balcony need for solar to be worth it?**

There is no hour threshold that makes solar work or not work — panels produce continuously, so the meaningful output is annual kilowatt-hours rather than a pass/fail. The common "three to four hours" rule comes from gardening advice and gives no method for finding out whether a given balcony clears it. In NYC, a typical 800 W system produces 400–900 kWh a year, worth roughly $136 to $306 at Con Edison's $0.34/kWh marginal rate.

**Do balcony solar panels work in winter in New York?**

Yes, but less. The real winter losses are short days (about 9h15m of daylight on 21 December against 15h06m in June), a sun that reaches only about 26 degrees above the horizon at solar noon, and inter-building shading — which is worst precisely when the sun is lowest. Cold weather does slightly improve cell efficiency, but that is the smallest term in the equation and it does not compensate for a balcony sitting in the shadow of the building opposite all day.

**Is a north-facing balcony worth solar panels?**

Sometimes, and more often than the widely repeated "75% less" figure implies — a claim we could not trace to any primary source. About 40% of the year's light in the Northeast is diffuse and reaches a north-facing panel regardless of orientation, and from late September to late March a north-facing wall gets no direct sun at all, so diffuse is most of what it lives on. In a dense city an unobstructed high-floor north balcony can out-produce a south-facing one boxed in by a taller building across a narrow street.

**Does my floor number really change the answer that much?**

Considerably, and often more than orientation does. With a six-storey building directly across a standard 60-foot Manhattan side street, a 2nd-floor balcony needs the sun above 37 degrees to see it at all — which never happens in December — while a 6th-floor balcony on the same facade needs only 6 degrees. Same building, same direction, very different year.

**Can I just watch my balcony to work out how much sun it gets?**

You can, but it takes a year to do properly and still returns hours rather than kilowatt-hours. The sun's path is known in advance and the surrounding buildings are in public data, so a shadow model answers the seasonal question immediately. Direct observation is best reserved for the things a model genuinely cannot see: a window AC unit above you, a corner tree, a deep parapet.

**Will an 800 W kit really cover 15–25% of my electricity?**

Usually not in New York. That figure is a nameplate-ideal one quoted with no shading derate applied. Against the EIA's New York average household consumption of about 6,850 kWh a year, the realistic 400–900 kWh NYC production band works out at roughly 6–13%, and a shaded low-floor balcony sits at the bottom of it.

# How to calculate balcony solar output and savings for any US address

URL: https://balco.nyc/calculate-balcony-solar-output  
Last reviewed: 2026-09-23

Take NREL’s PVWatts output for your location, tilt and direction. Multiply it by 0.95 for the railing and by a month-by-month shade factor for whatever stands opposite, then value each kWh at the price you actually stop paying. Worked through that chain with balco.nyc’s own PVWatts runs, an 800 W south-facing panel on a vertical railing makes 778 kWh a year in Phoenix, 616 in Chicago and 604 in New York City with an open view, and 328, 239 and 227 kWh on a third floor facing a six-to-ten-story building across a 20 m street. Shade changes the kWh more than the city does, and the price of a kWh decides the payback.

## The chain in one line, and what it gives for three cities

Every balcony solar estimate, including the one [the balco.nyc calculator](https://balco.nyc/) gives you, is a few multiplications and one loop:

- **kWh a year** = the sum over twelve months of (PVWatts monthly output × railing factor × that month’s shade factor)

- **Savings a year** = kWh × the price of a kWh you no longer buy

- **Payback** = years until cumulative savings reach the kit cost, with the price rising 3% and output falling 0.5% a year

- **CO₂ avoided** = kWh × your grid region’s emission rate

That is six steps, each with a number and a source, set out below so you can run the chain by hand or check another calculator against it. To show what it does, balco.nyc ran it for an 800 W system on a vertical, south-facing railing in three cities with very different sun and prices, using the site’s own PVWatts runs for each state’s largest city and its own shade code:

- **With an open view** the panel makes about **778 kWh a year in Phoenix, 616 in Chicago and 604 in New York City**. On a railing, Phoenix’s desert sun buys only 29% more than New York’s, against 37% more at a roof-style 35° tilt, because a vertical panel meets the high summer sun at a glancing angle.

- **From a third floor facing a six-to-ten-story building across a 20 m street**, the same panel loses 58% to 62% of that: **328, 239 and 227 kWh**. What stands opposite matters more than which city you are in.

- **Price matters more than sun.** At Con Edison’s 34¢ marginal rate the open New York panel saves $205 a year. At Arizona’s 15.4¢ average the Phoenix panel makes 29% more electricity and saves $120.

These are modeled figures for one reference point per city, not measurements. The full table is in section 5.

## Step 1: the sun and the panel’s geometry (PVWatts V8)

The first number is the one everything else multiplies: what the panel would make at this spot, tilt and direction with nothing in the way. balco.nyc gets it from NREL’s **PVWatts V8**, the Department of Energy’s reference production model, which simulates every hour of a typical meteorological year (TMY) drawn from the satellite-derived National Solar Radiation Database. The calculator sends these inputs:

| PVWatts input | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| system_capacity | 0.8 kW | Two 400 W panels (the calculator allows 0.4–1.6 kW) |
| tilt | 90° | Hung flat on a railing; 70°, 60° and 35° model angled brackets |
| azimuth | 180° | Due south (0 north, 90 east, 270 west) |
| module_type | 1 (premium) | PVWatts’s higher-efficiency crystalline module |
| array_type | 0 (fixed, open rack) | Air moves behind a railing panel, so it runs cooler than a roof-flush one |
| losses | 14% | PVWatts’s default total, which balco.nyc reads as wiring, mismatch, connections, nameplate and availability |
| soiling | 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3% by month | balco.nyc’s urban dust profile, heaviest in summer |
| dc_ac_ratio / inv_eff | 1.1 / 96.5% | A microinverter matched to one or two modules |
| albedo | 0.20 | A concrete balcony floor |

One caveat: PVWatts’s own manual builds its 14% default partly from 2% soiling and 3% shading, and balco.nyc applies soiling and shading again separately. Any overlap pushes the estimate down, not up.

For an 800 W vertical south panel PVWatts returns **819.4 kWh a year in Phoenix, 648.8 in Chicago and 635.7 in New York City**, before any railing loss. Tilted to 35° the same panel would make 1,369, 1,010 and 998 kWh, so a vertical railing keeps only **60% to 64%** of a rooftop-style figure. That ratio explains most inflated balcony estimates: they quote a tilted panel’s output for one that will hang straight down.

The monthly shape matters too. A vertical south panel is a winter machine: it meets the low winter sun almost head-on. In Phoenix it peaks at 104.7 kWh in December and bottoms out at 26.5 in June; in New York it runs from 73.0 in January to 31.9 in June. Winter is also when buildings opposite do the most damage. And a TMY is a typical year, not a forecast; any real year will differ.

## Steps 2 and 3: the railing, and the building across the street

**Step 2, the railing.** The railing, the mounting hardware and the slab above clip a rail-mounted panel’s lower edge, and PVWatts cannot see them. balco.nyc multiplies by **0.95 for a vertical panel** (0.97 at 70°, 0.98 at 60°, 0.99 at 35°). It is the site’s own assumption, not a measurement, and it applies to every estimate. Open-view output is therefore 819.4 × 0.95 = **778 kWh** in Phoenix, 616 in Chicago and 604 in New York.

**Step 3, the buildings opposite.** PVWatts assumes an open horizon, so the shade model answers one question: of the light PVWatts assumed, how much reaches this balcony? It starts from a horizon profile, the highest obstruction angle in each of 360 compass directions. In New York City the profile comes from real building footprints and heights within 200 m. Elsewhere it comes from your description, modeled as a continuous wall parallel to your facade:

> β(φ) = atan( (H − h) × cos φ / D ), with h = (floor − 1) × 3.05 m + 1.0 m

H is the height of the building opposite, h your balcony’s height, D the distance and φ the angle away from straight out. In the worked examples a third floor gives h = 7.1 m, “6 to 10 floors” is H = 25 m, and “across a street” is D = 20 m. Straight out, the wall rises to atan(17.9 / 20) = **41.8°** (32.3° at 45° either side). The winter-solstice noon sun reaches only about 33° in Phoenix, 25° in Chicago and 26° in New York. It clears 41.8° at noon only from about early March to early October in Chicago and New York, and early February to early November in Phoenix.

The shade factor comes from a sweep: on the 15th of each month, every 10 minutes from sunrise to sunset, light is split into beam (0.60) and diffuse (0.40). Beam counts only when the sun is above the horizon profile in its direction. Diffuse counts in proportion to the sky the panel can still see, which this wall cuts to 33%:

> shade factor = Σ received / Σ assumed, where received = beam × (sun visible) + diffuse × sky openness, and assumed = beam + diffuse

Hours with the sun behind the facade add almost nothing to either sum, since PVWatts has already priced orientation, so **an open view returns 1.00 at every orientation**, north included. Behind this wall New York’s factor is 0.73 in March, 0.54 in June and 0.72 in September. From October through February it falls to 0.10–0.12, with the sun below the wall all day. Three of those months sit at or just above the model’s floor of 0.10.

Apply the factors month by month, never as one annual average, because the shade is worst when a vertical panel produces most. In Phoenix the panel makes 373 kWh from November to February with an open view and 74 behind this wall: two-thirds of the year’s loss in four months. Multiplying by the plain average of Phoenix’s twelve factors (0.46) would overstate its shaded output by 10%. The month-by-month result is equivalent to 0.42 in Phoenix, 0.39 in Chicago and 0.38 in New York.

## Steps 4 to 6: the price of a kWh, payback and carbon

**Step 4, what a kWh is worth.** balco.nyc assumes every kWh is used at home, replacing one you would have bought. Over a year the volume is small: 604 kWh is under 9% of the average New York household’s 6,854 kWh. But self-consumption is decided hour by hour. When the panel makes more than the apartment is drawing, the surplus goes to the grid and is assumed to earn nothing unless your state or utility credits it, so the savings figure is a ceiling, not an expectation. Whether you may connect a panel at all varies by state and utility (see [the state pages](https://balco.nyc/states)). None of this is legal advice.

The right price is the *marginal* one: what one fewer kWh takes off your bill, meaning supply, delivery, surcharges and tax but not the fixed monthly charge. In New York City balco.nyc knows the tariff, so it uses **Con Edison’s 34¢/kWh** all-in marginal rate. That starts from Con Edison’s own SC-1 bill history (33.83¢ in 2025) and is [carried into 2026 here](https://balco.nyc/electricity-rate). Elsewhere it uses the state’s average residential price, which balco.nyc computes from EIA revenue and sales over the 12 months to June 2026: **15.40¢ in Arizona, 18.54¢ in Illinois, 27.96¢ in New York**. An average spreads fixed charges over every kWh, so it can overstate what an avoided kWh saves, and on tiered or time-of-use tariffs it can miss either way. It also blends utilities: New York’s statewide figure sits about six cents below Con Edison’s marginal rate. The best number is your own: a recent bill’s total minus fixed charges, divided by kWh billed. Enter it under Adjust assumptions, or as rate in a link.

**Step 5, payback.** The cost basis is balco.nyc’s mid-tier planning figure of $1,200 for 800 W ($850 budget, $1,600 premium), hardware only, with no electrical work. No federal credit is netted out: the residential clean energy credit (IRC 25D) ended with 2025. Simple payback is cost over first-year savings. The calculator’s figure comes from a loop, in nominal dollars with no discounting:

- Year 1 savings = kWh × price.

- Each later year, output falls 0.5% (degradation) and the price rises 3% (the default; 2% and 4% are presets).

- Add each year to a running total until it reaches the kit cost, then interpolate within that year.

For the open New York panel, year 1 saves 603.9 × $0.34 = $205.33. The next four years save $210.43, $215.66, $221.02 and $226.51, for $1,078.96 after five. Year 6 adds $232.14, and $1,200 is reached 52% of the way through it: **5.5 years**, against 5.8 simple.

**Step 6, carbon.** CO₂ avoided = kWh × the EPA eGRID2023 total output emission rate for the address’s grid subregion: 0.704 lb per kWh for WECC Southwest (Phoenix), 0.911 for RFC West (Chicago) and 0.864 for NYC/Westchester. eGRID’s non-baseload rates are higher in all three, so this is the conservative choice. Grid mix is why the Chicago panel avoids slightly more CO₂ than the Phoenix one (562 against 548 lb a year) while making 21% fewer kWh.

## Worked examples: Phoenix, Chicago and New York City

The whole chain side by side, for an 800 W vertical south panel at the $1,200 mid-tier cost, open and then from a third floor facing a six-to-ten-story building 20 m away. The shade step is balco.nyc’s own code run at each city’s latitude. In New York City the live calculator would use real footprints rather than a described wall; the wall is used here so the three cities are compared on equal terms. New York appears at Con Edison’s marginal rate, which the calculator uses, and at the EIA state average for comparison.

| Step | Phoenix, AZ | Chicago, IL | New York City | NYC at EIA state average |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. PVWatts, 90° south (kWh/yr) | 819.4 | 648.8 | 635.7 | 635.7 |
| 2. × 0.95 railing = open view (kWh) | 778 | 616 | 604 | 604 |
| 3. Shade factor, applied monthly (effective) | 0.42 | 0.39 | 0.38 | 0.38 |
| Shaded output (kWh) | 328 | 239 | 227 | 227 |
| 4. Price of a kWh | 15.40¢ (EIA avg) | 18.54¢ (EIA avg) | 34¢ (Con Ed marginal) | 27.96¢ (EIA avg) |
| Year-1 savings, open / shaded | $120 / $50 | $114 / $44 | $205 / $77 | $169 / $63 |
| 5. Payback, open (loop / simple) | 9.0 / 10.0 yrs | 9.4 / 10.5 yrs | 5.5 / 5.8 yrs | 6.6 / 7.1 yrs |
| Payback, shaded (loop / simple) | 18.9 / 23.8 yrs | 21.0 / 27.1 yrs | 13.3 / 15.6 yrs | 15.7 / 18.9 yrs |
| 25-year savings, open / shaded (nominal) | $4,087 / $1,720 | $3,896 / $1,512 | $7,000 / $2,629 | $5,757 / $2,162 |
| 6. CO₂ avoided, open / shaded (lb/yr) | 548 / 231 | 562 / 218 | 522 / 196 | 522 / 196 |

The shaded New York case month by month (PVWatts output × 0.95 × shade factor), so the sum can be checked:

| Month | PVWatts (kWh) | Shade factor | Result (kWh) | Month | PVWatts (kWh) | Shade factor | Result (kWh) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jan | 73.0 | 0.100 | 6.9 | Jul | 36.2 | 0.558 | 19.2 |
| Feb | 69.2 | 0.109 | 7.2 | Aug | 41.2 | 0.635 | 24.9 |
| Mar | 64.9 | 0.735 | 45.3 | Sep | 55.7 | 0.716 | 37.9 |
| Apr | 47.6 | 0.669 | 30.2 | Oct | 61.6 | 0.116 | 6.8 |
| May | 37.8 | 0.586 | 21.0 | Nov | 58.2 | 0.102 | 5.6 |
| Jun | 31.9 | 0.536 | 16.3 | Dec | 58.4 | 0.100 | 5.5 |

The total is **226.8 kWh**. Three things follow:

- **New York pays back fastest while making the fewest kWh**: 5.5 years open against Phoenix’s 9.0, and 13.3 shaded against 18.9. Price does that, not sun.

- **The choice of rate is worth a year.** The same New York panel pays back in 5.5 years at Con Edison’s marginal rate and 6.6 at the state average. A calculator that does not say which it used has hidden a result-changing input.

- **Heavy shade in a cheap-power state can eat most of a panel’s life.** Chicago’s shaded case needs 21 years on the loop. That argues for running your own address, not for giving up: a higher floor, a lower building or a wider street changes the answer quickly.

## The five numbers to check in any balcony solar calculator

A trustworthy balcony calculator shows five things. If any is missing, you cannot tell whether its answer is generous, cautious or wrong:

- **Annual kWh, with the tilt and direction behind it.** balco.nyc’s runs put an open 800 W vertical south panel at about 600–780 kWh across three very different cities. Near 1,000 kWh for a railing panel in the Northeast is probably a 35° rooftop number.

- **The electricity rate, and whether it is marginal.** Supply-only, average and all-in marginal rates answer different questions, and move the same New York panel’s payback by a year or more.

- **The shading method.** None, a flat percentage, or a horizon from real or described buildings, ideally applied by month. “No shading” on a low city floor is a best case, not an estimate.

- **The self-consumption assumption.** Whether every kWh is assumed to be used at home, and what surplus earns. Unless your state or utility credits exports, it earns nothing.

- **The cost basis.** Which kit price, whether wiring is included, and whether a tax credit was subtracted. The federal 25D credit ended with 2025.

balco.nyc states each of these with its estimates, and [the methodology](https://balco.nyc/methodology) documents every constant used above. To run your own address, start at [the calculator](https://balco.nyc/). To share an estimate, or have an assistant hand you one, use a prefilled link:

> https://balco.nyc/?address=STREET+ADDRESS,+CITY,+STATE&floor=3&facing=south&across=tall&distance=street

facing takes the eight compass points; across takes none, low, mid, tall or tower; distance takes alley, street, wide or far. Optional tilt, watts, bill and rate (cents per kWh from your bill) also work. Outside New York City, a link with address, floor, facing and across runs at once; in the city you still pin your balcony on the 3D model, because real buildings replace the description. State figures are on the [Arizona](https://balco.nyc/states/arizona), [Illinois](https://balco.nyc/states/illinois) and [New York](https://balco.nyc/states/new-york) pages, and [does my balcony get enough sun?](https://balco.nyc/balcony-sunlight) and [what balcony solar costs](https://balco.nyc/balcony-solar-cost) go deeper on shade and kit prices.

## Common questions

**How much electricity will an 800 W balcony solar panel produce in a year?**

It depends mostly on tilt and shade. balco.nyc's PVWatts runs put an 800 W south-facing panel hung vertically on a railing at about 778 kWh a year in Phoenix, 616 in Chicago and 604 in New York City with an open view, after a 5% railing loss. From a third floor facing a six-to-ten-story building across a 20 m street, the same panel makes about 328, 239 and 227 kWh.

**How do I calculate balcony solar output by hand?**

Take PVWatts' monthly output for your location, tilt and direction, multiply each month by 0.95 for a vertical railing mount and by that month's shade factor for the buildings opposite, and add the twelve months. PVWatts is NREL's free production model. The shade factor is the share of beam and diffuse light that still reaches the panel, and it equals 1.00 for an open view.

**Why are balcony solar estimates lower than rooftop solar estimates?**

Because a railing panel usually hangs vertically. In balco.nyc's PVWatts runs for Phoenix, Chicago and New York City, a vertical south-facing panel makes 60% to 64% of what the same panel tilted to 35 degrees would make, before any shading or railing loss. An estimate near 1,000 kWh a year for an 800 W railing panel in the Northeast is probably a tilted-panel figure.

**What electricity rate should I use to calculate balcony solar savings?**

Use the marginal rate: what one fewer kWh takes off your bill, including supply, delivery, surcharges and tax but excluding fixed monthly charges. To get it, subtract the fixed charges from a recent bill and divide by the kWh billed. In New York City balco.nyc uses Con Edison's all-in marginal rate of 34 cents; elsewhere it uses the EIA state average, which includes fixed charges and can overstate the value of an avoided kWh.

**How much does a building across the street reduce balcony solar output?**

It can more than halve it. In balco.nyc's model, a third-floor south-facing balcony facing a six-to-ten-story building 20 m away loses 58% to 62% of its annual output in Phoenix, Chicago and New York City. Most of the loss comes in winter, when the sun stays below the building opposite all day, and that is also when a vertical panel would produce the most.

**How is balcony solar payback calculated?**

Divide the kit cost by the first year's savings for a simple payback, or run a year-by-year loop in which output falls 0.5% and the electricity price rises 3% each year until cumulative savings reach the kit cost. For an unshaded 800 W vertical south panel in New York City at a $1,200 kit cost and Con Edison's 34-cent rate, balco.nyc gets 5.5 years on the loop and 5.8 years simple.

## Sources

- [NLR (formerly NREL) — PVWatts V8 API](https://developer.nlr.gov/docs/solar/pvwatts/v8/): the request parameters used in step 1 (module_type, array_type 0 “Fixed – Open Rack”, tilt, azimuth, losses, dc_ac_ratio, inv_eff, albedo, the 12-value monthly soiling array) and the ac_monthly and ac_annual outputs.
- [Dobos, PVWatts Version 5 Manual (NREL, 2014)](https://pvwatts.nlr.gov/downloads/pvwattsv5.pdf): the 14% default total system loss, and its components (including 2% soiling and 3% shading), behind the caveat in step 1.
- [NLR — National Solar Radiation Database (NSRDB) data](https://developer.nlr.gov/docs/solar/nsrdb/): the satellite-derived irradiance, with typical meteorological year products, that PVWatts simulates from.
- [EIA — Form EIA-861M monthly sales and revenue by state](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia861m/): the residential revenue and sales from which balco.nyc computes the 12-month state averages to June 2026: 15.40¢ Arizona, 18.54¢ Illinois, 27.96¢ New York.
- [EIA — 2024 Average Monthly Bill, Residential (Table 5A)](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/sales_revenue_price/pdf/table_5A.pdf): average New York household consumption of 571 kWh a month (about 6,854 a year), used for the self-consumption comparison in step 4.
- [Con Edison — historical average full-service electric rates](https://www.coned.com/-/media/files/coned/documents/save-energy-money/using-private-generation/historical-average-full-service-electric-rates.pdf): the NYC SC-1 residential rate of 33.83¢/kWh in 2025 that the 34¢ marginal rate starts from.
- [EPA — eGRID2023 Summary Tables (revision 2, June 2025)](https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2025-06/summary_tables_rev2.pdf): subregion total output CO₂ rates of 703.7 (WECC Southwest), 911.4 (RFC West) and 864.5 lb/MWh (NYC/Westchester), and the higher non-baseload rates.
- [IRS — Residential Clean Energy Credit](https://www.irs.gov/credits-deductions/residential-clean-energy-credit): that the credit is not available for property placed in service after December 31, 2025, so none is netted out of the cost basis.
